State general fund revenues decrease beginning in fiscal 2025 from reduced collection commissions remitted by clerks of the circuit court. State expenditures are unaffected, and local reporting requirements can be absorbed with existing resources; exact revenue loss figures are unavailable because transaction volume and values cannot be reliably predicted.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: In 10 Maryland counties, the Clerks of the Circuit Court (supported operationally and administratively by the Administrative Office of the Courts) collect local recordation taxes and retain a percentage commission that is remitted to the State General Fund. Under this bill, circuit court clerks in these jurisdictions are responsible for implementing the altered exemption threshold, will see a decrease in collected commissions, and are mandated to compile and submit annual reports to the General Assembly regarding the exempt mortgages and forgone tax revenue.

qa_results.bill_summary: Renames the Veterans of the Afghanistan and Iraq Conflicts Scholarship to the Douglas J. J. Peters Veterans of the Afghanistan and Iraq Conflicts Scholarship. Alters the name of the associated nonlapsing scholarship fund accordingly. Maintains fund administration and annual reporting requirements under the Maryland Higher Education Commission. Takes effect July 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: veterans and active-duty members of the U.S. Armed Forces who served in the Afghanistan and Iraq conflicts, activated reserve and Maryland National Guard members, and their eligible spouses, children, and stepchildren
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures can be absorbed within existing budgeted resources. State revenues are not affected, and there is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHEC administers the Veterans of the Afghanistan and Iraq Conflicts Scholarship and its associated fund, and will be responsible for implementing the name change across its systems (such as the Maryland College Aid Processing System) and reporting.
The Commission directly oversees and administers the scholarship program and scholarship fund being renamed by this legislation.
The Comptroller is statutorily designated to account for the newly renamed Douglas J. J. Peters Veterans of the Afghanistan and Iraq Conflicts Scholarship Fund.
The State Treasurer is statutorily designated to hold the Douglas J. J. Peters Veterans of the Afghanistan and Iraq Conflicts Scholarship Fund separately and receive deposits for the fund.

qa_results.bill_summary: Regulates audits of pharmacies and pharmacists conducted by pharmacy benefits managers and authorized auditing entities. Requires the Secretary of Health to adopt pharmacy audit regulations for pharmacy benefits managers contracting with managed care organizations. Prohibits pharmacy benefits managers from auditing more than 125 prescriptions during a desk or site audit. Bars managers from recouping funds for incorrect days-of-supply calculations when package sizes are unbreakable. Requires managers to accept completed cash register transactions as proof of pickup unless contradictory information exists. Mandates managers respond to audit inquiries within three business days and provide secure electronic document submission mechanisms.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health; Maryland Insurance Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Pharmacies, pharmacists, pharmacy benefits managers, auditing entities, Medicaid managed care organizations, and health benefit plan purchasers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Indeterminate expenditure increase for the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program and Medicaid managed care organizations if pharmacy benefits managers pass increased administrative costs to purchasers, with an indeterminate increase in federal matching revenues. Local government expenditures for fully insured health plans may also increase. Specific figures are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Secretary of Health to adopt regulations establishing audit standards for pharmacy benefits managers (PBMs) contracting with Medicaid managed care organizations (MCOs), which may also result in an increase in Medicaid expenditures.

The bill amends Insurance Article § 15-1629, which is regulated and enforced by the Maryland Insurance Administration, granting the Insurance Commissioner regulatory authority over PBM audit standards and procedures.

DBM administers the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program, which contracts with PBMs; any additional administrative costs incurred by PBMs complying with the new audit restrictions may be passed along to the State Plan.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits health insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and health maintenance organizations from imposing cost-sharing for diagnostic and supplemental breast examinations. Authorizes carriers to apply deductible requirements to these examinations for enrollees covered under high-deductible health plans. Requires the Maryland Health Care Commission to study eliminating cost-sharing for diagnostic image-guided breast cancer biopsies. Directs the commission to submit its report to the Governor and legislative committees by October 1, 2023. Applies the cost-sharing prohibition to health benefit plans issued, delivered, or renewed on or after January 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Health Care Commission; Maryland Insurance Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Insurers, nonprofit health service plans, health maintenance organizations, individuals receiving diagnostic or supplemental breast cancer examinations, and local governments purchasing health plans
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Minimal increase in Maryland Insurance Administration special fund revenues in FY 2024 from $125 rate and form filing fees. Form reviews and the Maryland Health Care Commission study will be conducted within existing budgeted resources. Local government expenditures may increase to the extent that fully insured employee health plans face higher premium costs, but exact figures are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Section 2 of the bill directly mandates that the Maryland Health Care Commission study and submit a report to the Governor and legislative committees on the financial impact of eliminating health insurance cost-sharing for diagnostic image-guided biopsies for breast cancer.

As the state's insurance regulator, MIA is responsible for enforcing compliance with the new coverage and cost-sharing prohibitions under the Insurance Article, as well as reviewing carriers' rate and form filings.

DBM administers the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program, which may experience an indeterminate fiscal impact from prohibiting cost-sharing on diagnostic and supplemental breast examinations.
MHBE oversees qualified health plans offered on the individual and small group exchange in Maryland, which are subject to state insurance coverage mandates and cost-sharing requirements.

qa_results.bill_summary: Increases the contract value threshold requiring competitive bidding by the Friendship Heights Village Council from $5,000 to $20,000. Authorizes the village council, by majority vote, to award contracts exceeding $20,000 without competitive bids during an emergency. Defines an emergency as an unforeseeable condition requiring action to mitigate serious damage to public health, safety, or welfare. Permits the village council to engage in cooperative procurement with other Montgomery County governmental entities. Takes effect October 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Friendship Heights Village Council
qa_results.stakeholders: Friendship Heights Village Council, residents of the Village of Friendship Heights special taxing district, and contractors bidding on village procurements
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state fiscal effect. Has limited or no fiscal impact on the Village of Friendship Heights, but provides operational and administrative efficiencies for emergency responses.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Office of Financial Regulation under the Commissioner of Financial Regulation in the Maryland Department of Labor. Requires the Commissioner to appoint a Deputy Commissioner for Depository Activities and a Deputy Commissioner for Non-Depository Activities. Requires each deputy commissioner to possess at least five years of specified regulatory or management experience. Prohibits the Commissioner and deputy commissioners from engaging in certain outside banking or lending businesses. Clarifies that renaming the office does not alter the powers or duties of the Commissioner.
qa_results.responsible_party: Commissioner of Financial Regulation; Maryland Department of Labor
qa_results.stakeholders: Depository financial institutions, non-depository financial entities regulated or licensed in Maryland, and staff of the Office of Financial Regulation
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No effect on revenues. One-time costs for revising signage and ongoing salary and benefit costs for the new deputy commissioner position can be absorbed within existing budgeted resources. No local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly reorganizes and renames an internal agency unit, establishing the Office of Financial Regulation within the Maryland Department of Labor and creating two distinct Deputy Commissioner positions (Depository and Non-Depository Activities) appointed by the Commissioner with the approval of the Secretary of Labor.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Maryland Department of Health and the Prescription Drug Affordability Board jointly to study Medicaid prescription drug claims. Directs the entities to compare managed care organization payments to fee-for-service rates for calendar years 2021 and 2022. Requires recommendations on addressing reimbursement inconsistencies by evaluating total State costs. Requires recommended methodologies for determining the most accurate drug ingredient costs and appropriate dispensing fees. Mandates a joint report of findings to the Maryland Medicaid Administration and specified legislative committees by October 31, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health; Prescription Drug Affordability Board
qa_results.stakeholders: Medicaid managed care organizations, pharmacies participating in the Maryland Medical Assistance Program, and pharmacy benefits managers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health and the Prescription Drug Affordability Board can conduct the study and report findings using existing budgeted resources. State revenues and local finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Maryland Department of Health (Medicaid Administration) to jointly conduct a study on managed care organization prescription drug claims and fee-for-service reimbursement rates, and report its findings and recommendations by October 31, 2023.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that the Prescription Drug Affordability Board, an independent state board, jointly conduct the study and issue findings and recommendations alongside the Maryland Department of Health.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits an institution of higher education from withholding a transcript because a current or former student owes a debt. Bars institutions from conditioning transcript issuance on debt payment. Prohibits institutions from charging higher transcript fees or providing less favorable treatment because a student owes a debt. Forbids institutions from using transcript issuance as a debt collection tool. Defines debt to include institutional credit and guaranteed nonfederal education loans. Excludes fees charged for the actual costs of providing a transcript from the definition of debt.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland institutions of higher education
qa_results.stakeholders: Current and former college students with outstanding student debt; public, private nonprofit, and for-profit institutions of higher education; and the Central Collection Unit.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Potential, indeterminate decrease in debt collection revenues for public four-year institutions, Baltimore City Community College, local community colleges, and the Central Collection Unit. Institutions may partially offset forgone revenue by raising tuition and fees for future students. Expenditures are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly applies to institutions of higher education within the University System of Maryland, prohibiting them from withholding transcripts or conditioning their release on the payment of student debt, which will impact institutional debt collection policies and potentially reduce revenues.

As an independent public four-year university, Morgan State University is directly bound by the prohibition on withholding transcripts for unpaid student debts, which may affect its debt collection practices and revenues.

As a public institution of higher education, St. Mary's College is subject to the bill's provisions barring punitive transcript measures for student debt, directly impacting its student account and collection procedures.

As the State's central regulatory and coordinating agency for higher education policies and institutions, MHEC is relevant to the statewide implementation and oversight of academic and administrative standards affecting postsecondary institutions.

The Central Collection Unit (CCU), housed within DBM, collects delinquent student debt on behalf of public institutions of higher education. The fiscal note indicates CCU collection revenues could decrease due to the removal of transcript holds as an enforcement tool.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state higher education institutions regarding compliance with the new statutory restriction and houses the Consumer Protection Division, which monitors educational debt practices.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a commercial blue and flathead catfish finfish trotline license in Maryland tidal waters. Authorizes licensees to catch blue and flathead catfish for sale using a finfish trotline. Sets an annual license fee of $15 for a term running September 1 through August 31. Exempts applicants from the requirement to hold a tidal fish license to be eligible. Allows licensees to purchase a seafood dealer authorization at a reduced fee of $50.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources
qa_results.stakeholders: commercial fishers harvesting blue and flathead catfish and seafood dealers in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund revenues to the Fisheries Research and Development Fund increase by up to $1,500 in fiscal 2023 and approximately $1,500 annually thereafter from license fees. Expenditures for the Department of Natural Resources are not affected, as the department can administer the license with existing budgeted resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: House Bill 386 establishes a commercial blue and flathead catfish finfish trotline license administered directly by the Department of Natural Resources (DNR). DNR is responsible for processing applications, adopting regulations, issuing the licenses, and collecting the associated licensing fees deposited into the Fisheries Research and Development Fund.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Board of Public Works to give notice of State bond sales through the Municipal Market Monitor. Allows notice through a similar service or another method the State Treasurer deems appropriate. Replaces Munifacts News Service with the Municipal Market Monitor for postponed bond sale notices. Requires postponed sale notices at least 24 hours before the new submission deadline. Takes effect June 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Board of Public Works; State Treasurer
qa_results.stakeholders: Prospective bidders on State bonds and municipal bond market participants
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Potential minimal decrease in State general fund expenditures by enabling the use of less costly notification methods, with no impact on revenues or local finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly authorizes the State Treasurer to determine the appropriate service or method (such as the Municipal Market Monitor) for public notice of State bond sales and postponed sales, and could result in minor expenditure savings for bond advertising.

The bill explicitly authorizes the Board of Public Works to give public notice of the public sale of State bonds through the Municipal Market Monitor (TM3) or other methods deemed appropriate by the State Treasurer.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the State Specialist for Value-Added Agriculture as a position within the Maryland Department of Agriculture. Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to appoint the specialist. Directs the specialist to serve as the primary contact and regulatory liaison for value-added agricultural enterprises. Focuses the specialist's first-year priority on implementing recommendations from the state meat process inspection task force. Mandates the creation of a Position Identification Number for the position within the department.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Agriculture
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland farmers, agricultural producers, processors, and value-added agricultural businesses
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $81,500 in FY 2024 and between $97,400 and $111,800 annually through FY 2028 to fund one new specialist position and operating costs. Revenues and local finances are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a statutory position within the Maryland Department of Agriculture—the State Specialist for Value-Added Agriculture—appointed by the Secretary of Agriculture. MDA is the primary implementing agency and receives an additional position identification number (PIN) and state general fund expenditures to hire and support the specialist.

As the state's central personnel and budget agency, DBM is responsible for authorizing the creation of the new Position Identification Number (PIN) and administering salary and benefit allocations established by the bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires parking citations issued by political subdivisions, State agencies, or third-party contractors to include a plate discrepancy checkbox. Allows cited individuals to check the box indicating registration plates were not issued for the described vehicle. Mandates that issuing entities verify liability through the Motor Vehicle Administration upon receiving a checked citation. Authorizes issuing entities to contact the cited person during the verification process. Requires dismissal of the citation if verification shows the person should not be held liable. Prohibits submitting a citation with the box checked if the plates match the described vehicle.
qa_results.responsible_party: Motor Vehicle Administration; Maryland State agencies; Maryland political subdivisions
qa_results.stakeholders: Vehicle owners and drivers receiving parking citations, political subdivisions, State agencies, and third-party parking enforcement contractors
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State and local expenditures increase in fiscal 2024 to reprint or modify citations and manage verification requests, though exact costs cannot be reliably estimated. Parking revenues may be delayed but are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires political subdivisions, State agencies, or contractors to verify vehicle registration and plate information through the Administration (MVA) when a cited person checks the box indicating the plates were not issued for the vehicle.
MDOT is the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration and oversees State transportation laws under the Transportation Article being amended.

DGS manages State-owned facilities, parking lots, and operates the Maryland Capitol Police, which enforces parking regulations and will need to update citation stock/software and handle verification requests.
MSP issues vehicle citations and will be required to update its parking citation forms to include the required check box and follow the verification process.

The District Court adjudicates contested parking citations; the bill's verification and dismissal mechanism prior to court appearance could result in a negligible reduction in court trials for contested citations.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the State Treasurer or designee to send written notice of a tort claim denial by e-mail. Authorizes notice by regular mail if regular mail is the only available means of notifying the claimant. Repeals the requirement that final denial notices be sent by certified mail, return receipt requested. Applies to notices sent to claimants or their legal representatives or counsel. Takes effect June 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Treasurer
qa_results.stakeholders: Claimants filing claims under the Maryland Tort Claims Act and their legal representatives or counsel
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for postage and handling decrease by approximately $17,800 annually beginning in FY 2024. Revenues and local government finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Treasurer's Office is the primary implementing agency responsible for processing claims under the Maryland Tort Claims Act and administering the State Insurance Trust Fund. The bill directly alters the statutory requirement for how the Treasurer sends denial notices, enabling the office to send notices by email or regular mail and saving an estimated $17,800 annually in postage and handling.

The Office of the Attorney General represents the State in tort litigation and advises the Treasurer regarding MTCA claims and settlements. The method and timing of claim denials can impact subsequent tort litigation and statute of limitations defenses handled by the Attorney General's office.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes notice, public hearing, and reporting requirements before an Executive Branch principal department closes or changes a State facility. Expands the definition of State facility to include any facility where 25 or more State employees are regularly assigned. Requires a principal department to make an explanatory report publicly available at least 270 days before a closure hearing. Mandates advance notices to the public, local General Assembly members, and exclusive bargaining representatives before closures or use changes. Authorizes departments to modify timelines during emergencies that pose health or safety risks to facility employees, patients, or inmates.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Executive Branch Principal Departments
qa_results.stakeholders: State employees, exclusive representatives of bargaining unit employees, patients, inmates, residents of State facilities, and local communities
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures and operations may be minimally affected to the extent facility closures or operational changes are delayed, but costs can likely be absorbed with existing budgeted resources. No local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DGS is the state's central real estate, leasing, and facility management agency. The bill sets rigorous notice, reporting, and public hearing procedures for acquiring, leasing, changing the use of, or closing state facilities with 25 or more employees or those providing health, juvenile, or correctional services.

MDH operates state healthcare and residential treatment facilities providing health services to clients, which are specifically subject to the bill's procedural requirements before modifying facility use, leasing new property, or executing closures.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS operates state correctional facilities and detention centers. The bill specifically governs facilities providing correctional services to inmates, establishing extensive notice, public hearing, and transition reporting requirements before closing or altering their purpose.

DJS operates state residential and detention facilities providing juvenile services to youth, which are expressly covered by the bill's enhanced notice, public hearing, and reporting mandates for facility closures and operational changes.

As the state's central personnel and budget agency, DBM is impacted by requirements to analyze the budgetary impacts of closures, coordinate notice with employee exclusive representatives, and assist state employees affected by facility closures in finding other employment.

Principal departments of the Executive Branch planning to close a state facility are required by the bill to submit a comprehensive closure report directly to the Governor outlining reasons, budgetary impacts, employee transition plans, and future facility plans.

The Board of Public Works approves major state leases, property acquisitions, capital projects, and transfers of state-owned real estate that result when state facilities are acquired, repurposed, or closed.

qa_results.bill_summary: Repeals the statutory 10% limit on investments in commercial paper for State unexpended or surplus funds. Requires the State Treasurer to adopt regulations establishing a State investment policy by December 1, 2023. Directs the regulations to specify maximum investment thresholds for each authorized asset class. Requires the State Treasurer to notify the leadership of covered local governmental units in writing. Permits affected local governments to review, revise, and report changes in their local investment policies.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Treasurer
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland local governments (including Baltimore City, counties, municipalities, community colleges, Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission, and debt-issuing authorities and public corporations) and the State Treasurer's Office
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Potential indeterminate increase in State general fund revenues beginning in FY 2024 to the extent higher investment returns are realized from commercial paper. State expenditures are unaffected. Local government revenues may be minimally affected by potentially higher investment returns, with no impact on local expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly governs the State Treasurer's authority to invest unexpended and surplus State funds. It repeals statutory percentage caps on commercial paper investments, mandates that the Treasurer adopt regulations establishing an investment policy with thresholds for each authorized asset class, and requires the Treasurer to notify and consult with local government units regarding local investment policy updates.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency is referenced in the section of law being amended regarding its ongoing joint responsibilities with the Treasurer to develop guidelines and receive annual reporting on the utilization of minority business enterprises for brokerage and investment management services, though the bill does not alter these existing statutory duties.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the definition of practice audiology to include prescribing, ordering, selling, dispensing, or fitting hearing aids or osseo-integrated devices. Defines osseo-integrated device as a bone-anchored hearing device or cochlear implants. Expands hearing aid dispensing to include ordering suitable hearing instruments, including prescription hearing aids. Excludes the servicing, marketing, sale, dispensing, customer support, or distribution of authorized over-the-counter hearing aids from state regulation. Takes effect July 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Examiners for Audiologists, Hearing Aid Dispensers, Speech-Language Pathologists, and Music Therapists
qa_results.stakeholders: Audiologists, hearing aid dispensers, consumers using hearing instruments or osseo-integrated devices, and retailers of over-the-counter hearing aids
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The State Board of Examiners for Audiologists, Hearing Aid Dispensers, Speech-Language Pathologists, and Music Therapists can update regulations with existing budgeted resources. Revenues are unaffected, and there is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Maryland Audiology, Hearing Aid Dispensing, Speech-Language Pathology, and Music Therapy Act under the Health Occupations Article. The licensing board governing these professionals—the State Board of Examiners for Audiologists, Hearing Aid Dispensers, Speech-Language Pathologists, and Music Therapists—operates within the Maryland Department of Health, which will be responsible for updating regulations to conform to these statutory changes.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency advocates for the welfare and policy interests of Maryland residents who are deaf or hard of hearing, making statutory definitions and regulatory exemptions regarding hearing aids, prescription hearing instruments, and osseo-integrated devices relevant to its mission.

qa_results.bill_summary: Adds a nonvoting student member to the Kent County Board of Education. Requires the member to be a county resident, a high school junior or senior, and a student government member. Establishes an election process where county high school students vote directly before May 1 each year. Sets a one-year term beginning July 1 and requires the student to advise the board on student perspectives. Prohibits the student member from attending executive sessions unless invited by a majority vote of the board.
qa_results.responsible_party: Kent County Board of Education
qa_results.stakeholders: High school students in Kent County and members of the Kent County Board of Education
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state or local fiscal impact because the bill codifies existing practice.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Education Article regarding the composition and governance of the Kent County Board of Education, a local school system under the regulatory oversight and leadership of the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) and the State Board of Education.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes Baltimore City, counties, and municipal corporations to alter the limitation on a homeowner's combined gross income. Applies this authority to local supplements for the State Homeowners' Property Tax Credit Program. Allows local jurisdictions to expand credit eligibility to homeowners with higher household incomes. Requires local governments to notify the State Department of Assessments and Taxation of any enacted changes. Takes effect June 1, 2023, applicable to taxable years beginning after June 30, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation; Baltimore City; Maryland counties; Maryland municipal corporations
qa_results.stakeholders: homeowners with combined gross incomes exceeding standard thresholds, Baltimore City, Maryland counties, and Maryland municipal corporations
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state fiscal effect as the State Department of Assessments and Taxation administers supplements within existing resources. Local property tax revenues may decrease beginning in fiscal 2024 to the extent local governments expand credit eligibility, with specific revenue losses varying by jurisdiction.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board (PTAAB) is responsible for hearing administrative appeals regarding real property assessments, exemptions, and property tax credit determinations administered through the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT). Altering eligibility criteria and income limits for local homeowners' property tax credit supplements may minimally impact the volume of appeals heard by local boards.

The Maryland Tax Court adjudicates appeals arising from final decisions of local taxing authorities and the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board, including disputes related to property tax assessments and credits.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires persons not required to be licensed or permitted under wildlife law to obtain a free Department identification number. Applies the requirement before using a snare, a trap, or another similar device to capture wildlife. Requires users to stamp the identification number on the device or on an affixed metal tag. Authorizes the Department to waive this requirement for devices used only on owned or rented private property. Authorizes anyone who finds a noncompliant device to report it to the Department or Natural Resources Police Force.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources; Natural Resources Police Force
qa_results.stakeholders: individuals using snares, traps, or similar devices to capture wildlife who are exempt from licensing or permitting; private landowners and tenants trapping wildlife on their property
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances and operations are not materially affected. The Department of Natural Resources can issue additional identification numbers using its existing COMPASS licensing system within existing budgeted resources. Revenue from existing penalties is not anticipated to have a material impact, and local governments are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) by requiring trappers exempt from licensing to obtain a free DNR identification number through its electronic system (COMPASS). It also authorizes DNR to grant identification waivers on certain private lands and tasks DNR and the Natural Resources Police Force with receiving reports and enforcing compliance regarding nonconforming snares and traps.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits local boards of elections from voting to change polling place locations without holding a public meeting with testimony. Requires local boards to submit a polling place plan to the State Board of Elections before statewide primary elections. Requires the State Board of Elections to reject plans that negatively affect access for historically disenfranchised communities. Expands criminal and civil prohibitions against influencing a voter's decision whether to vote by other lawful means. Moves the 2024 statewide and Baltimore City municipal primary election date to the second Tuesday in May.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections; local boards of elections
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland registered voters, historically disenfranchised communities, local boards of elections, and elected municipal, county, and state officials
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $156,400 in FY 2024 and between $109,400 and $164,500 annually thereafter for a program administrator and mapping services. Local government expenditures increase collectively by at least $37,500 in FY 2024, with similar recurring costs in primary election years, to cover local cost shares for mapping services and plan development.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Elections (SBE) is the primary regulatory agency responsible for administering the bill's provisions, including reviewing and approving local polling place plans, procuring mapping services, and overseeing the rescheduled 2024 primary election date.

The Office of the State Prosecutor is responsible for investigating and prosecuting election law violations and is directly impacted by the bill's expansion of criminal prohibitions against influencing voters' decisions to vote by any lawful means.
The judiciary is responsible for handling any civil penalty adjudications or criminal misdemeanor proceedings resulting from violations of the expanded prohibited election acts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender may represent indigent defendants charged under the expanded criminal provisions regarding election interference and voter intimidation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department would be responsible for housing and supervising individuals convicted of misdemeanor voter intimidation offenses that carry penalties of up to five years of imprisonment.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits an incarcerated person from violating any pretrial or posttrial condition banning contact, harassment, or abuse of an alleged victim. Forbids covered individuals from entering or approaching an alleged victim's residence or place of employment. Applies to defendants charged with sex crimes against minors, crimes of violence, domestic offenses, or stalking. Classifies a violation as a misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment not exceeding 90 days. Takes effect October 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Judiciary of Maryland; Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
qa_results.stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals and criminal defendants charged with specified offenses; alleged victims of crimes of violence, stalking, domestic abuse, and sexual crimes against minors
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local finances or operations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly applies to incarcerated individuals in state correctional and pretrial detention facilities, prohibiting them from violating conditions that bar contact or harassment of alleged victims.
The courts establish pretrial and posttrial release conditions and will adjudicate misdemeanor charges resulting from violations of this section.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates criminal misdemeanor liability subject to up to 90 days imprisonment, requiring indigent defense representation by the Office of the Public Defender for individuals charged under this statute.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Behavioral Health Workforce Investment Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund administered by the Maryland Department of Health. Directs the fund to reimburse costs associated with educating, training, certifying, recruiting, placing, and retaining behavioral health professionals and paraprofessionals. Requires the Maryland Health Care Commission to conduct a comprehensive behavioral health workforce needs assessment by October 1, 2024. Directs the Commission to recommend an initial fund allocation and submit the assessment by October 15, 2024. Requires the Department to submit an annual fund utilization report beginning December 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health; Maryland Health Care Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: behavioral health professionals and paraprofessionals, behavioral health healthcare providers, local health departments, and higher education institutions
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund expenditures for the Maryland Health Care Commission increase by $75,000 in FY 2024 to conduct the needs assessment. General fund expenditures and special fund revenues are estimated to increase by at least $1.0 million annually beginning in FY 2025 to capitalize the fund, with corresponding special fund expenditures for provider reimbursements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Department of Health (MDH) to administer the newly established Behavioral Health Workforce Investment Fund and submit an annual report detailing fund disbursements and workforce metrics. MDH's Behavioral Health Administration is also tasked with coordinating on the workforce needs assessment.

The bill mandates MHCC to conduct a comprehensive behavioral health workforce needs assessment by October 1, 2024, recommend initial fund allocations, and report findings to legislative committees, resulting in a direct special fund expenditure of $75,000 in FY 2024.

MHEC is statutorily designated to coordinate with MHCC in conducting the comprehensive behavioral health workforce needs assessment, and may also receive special fund revenues/reimbursements to support training and education programs.
The Maryland Department of Labor is explicitly required by statute to coordinate with MHCC on the comprehensive behavioral health workforce needs assessment.
The State Treasurer is statutorily required to hold the Behavioral Health Workforce Investment Fund separately and invest its moneys with interest credited back to the fund.
The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to account for the newly created Behavioral Health Workforce Investment Fund.
The bill specifies that the new Behavioral Health Workforce Investment Fund is subject to audit by the Office of Legislative Audits.
USM institutions that provide higher education and clinical training for behavioral health professionals may be eligible for reimbursement or grant funding from the new fund.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Health Services Cost Review Commission to evaluate the reasonableness of hospital rates consistent with the all-payer model contract. Permits the Commission to take into account objective standards of efficiency and effectiveness under the contract terms. Applies to the Commission's review and approval of rates and revenues set or requested by health care facilities. Takes effect October 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Health Services Cost Review Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Hospitals, health care facilities, and purchasers of health care facility services in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state or local fiscal impact, as the bill codifies existing practices of the Health Services Cost Review Commission.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly governs the Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC), specifying that when the Commission determines the reasonableness of hospital rates using objective standards of efficiency and effectiveness, it must do so in a manner consistent with the all-payer model contract.

HSCRC is an independent commission established within the Maryland Department of Health under the Health - General Article, and rate-setting functions coordinate with state health policy and model programs administered alongside the Secretary of Health.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the State Retirement and Pension System to pay regular interest on nonvested member accounts. Covers former nonvested members who are currently active members of one of the several systems. Applies only if the individual has not withdrawn accumulated contributions and lacks a vested allowance. Mandates regular interest to accrue while the individual remains an active member of a system. Applies retroactively to the date an individual rejoined if active on July 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Retirement and Pension System; State Retirement Agency
qa_results.stakeholders: Active members of the State Retirement and Pension System who have nonvested accounts from previous system membership, the State of Maryland, and participating governmental units.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State and participating governmental unit pension liabilities increase minimally due to approximately $514,000 in retroactive interest payments across about 1,600 accounts, resulting in a negligible increase in annual employer pension contributions and no effect on revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 424 directly governs the administration of interest on nonvested accounts for active members within the State Retirement and Pension System (SRPS), which the Maryland State Retirement Agency administers and operates.

As the central personnel and fiscal agency managing state employee benefits and overall state employer pension contribution impacts, DBM is minimally impacted by the minor adjustments to pension liabilities and contributions.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters criminal immunity provisions for individuals experiencing a medical emergency after ingesting or using alcohol or drugs. Applies immunity from arrest, charge, or prosecution directly to a person experiencing a medical emergency. Prohibits sanctions for violating pretrial release, probation, or parole conditions against a person experiencing a medical emergency. Protects qualifying individuals when evidence arises solely from seeking, providing, assisting with, or receiving medical assistance. Covers specified violations relating to controlled dangerous substances, drug paraphernalia, and underage alcohol offenses.
qa_results.responsible_party: Judiciary; Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services; Department of State Police
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals experiencing medical emergencies after ingesting or using alcohol or drugs, individuals seeking or assisting with medical assistance, individuals on pretrial release, probation, or parole, and law enforcement officers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local finances or operations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS oversees the Division of Parole and Probation as well as pretrial detention and release services. The bill directly impacts their operations by establishing that individuals experiencing a drug- or alcohol-related medical emergency may not be sanctioned for violations of conditions of pretrial release, probation, or parole based on evidence obtained from receiving medical assistance.

As the primary state law enforcement agency enforcing criminal and drug laws across Maryland, MSP officers are directly governed by the statutory immunity provisions prohibiting arrest and charging for specified controlled substance and alcohol violations during medical emergencies.

AOC supports the Maryland Judiciary, where judges preside over criminal proceedings, establish pretrial release and probation conditions, and adjudicate alleged violations and prosecutions governed by the statutory immunity amendments.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: OPD represents indigent individuals in criminal prosecutions, bail/pretrial hearings, and probation/parole revocation proceedings. The expansion of statutory immunity provides a direct legal defense against arrests, charges, and revocation sanctions for their clients.
The OAG advises state agencies on legal standards, represents the State in criminal appeals, and provides guidance regarding the interpretation and application of statutory criminal immunity laws.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the University System of Maryland Board of Regents to award a grant to first-year student members. Permits the University System of Maryland Foundation to distribute restricted private donor funds directly or through constituent institutions. Caps the grant amount at the cost of tuition and fees incurred during the member's first year. Prohibits the grant from causing total financial aid to exceed the annual cost of attendance. Specifies that the grant or second-year tuition waiver does not constitute a gift, compensation, or university employment.
qa_results.responsible_party: University System of Maryland Board of Regents; University System of Maryland Foundation
qa_results.stakeholders: Student members of the University System of Maryland Board of Regents
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Higher education revenues and expenditures increase by offsetting amounts if private donations are received and distributed for student grants. Grants may range from standard undergraduate tuition up to graduate program costs, with no net general fund impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly applies to the University System of Maryland (USM) Board of Regents, authorizing it to provide a privately funded grant to cover tuition and fees for the student member of the board during the first year of a two-year term.

The bill creates an explicit statutory exclusion under the Maryland Public Ethics Law (Title 5 of the General Provisions Article), stipulating that the authorized grant or tuition waiver provided to the student regent shall not be considered a prohibited gift or compensation.

qa_results.bill_summary: Adds the Comptroller and the Attorney General as members of the Procurement Improvement Council. Authorizes the Comptroller and the Attorney General to each send a designee to meetings if unable to attend. Expands the statutory duties of the Council regarding vendor participation. Requires the Council to discuss strategies to increase participation of small, minority-owned, and women-owned businesses in procurement contracts. Takes effect October 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Procurement Improvement Council; Comptroller of Maryland; Maryland Office of the Attorney General
qa_results.stakeholders: State procurement agencies and officials, the Comptroller, the Attorney General, and small, minority-owned, and women-owned businesses
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not affect State or local finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Chief Procurement Officer, housed within the Department of General Services, serves as the Chairman and principal staff of the Procurement Improvement Council, which is directly altered and governed by this bill.
The bill directly adds the Comptroller to the membership of the Procurement Improvement Council and authorizes the Comptroller to send a designee to meetings.
The bill directly adds the Attorney General to the membership of the Procurement Improvement Council and authorizes the Attorney General to send a designee to meetings.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Special Secretary is a statutory member of the Council, and the bill explicitly adds a council duty to discuss strategies to increase the participation of small, minority-owned, and women-owned businesses in State procurement contracts.
The Procurement Advisor of the Board sits on the Council, and the Council is statutorily tasked with advising the Board of Public Works on procurement issues and recommending improvements.
The State Treasurer is a statutory member of the Procurement Improvement Council, whose membership and meeting designee provisions are detailed in the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Procurement Improvement Council is an advisory and coordinative council established to evaluate and improve State procurement practices.
The Governor appoints several members of the Procurement Improvement Council with the advice and consent of the Senate.

qa_results.bill_summary: Increases the number of full-time assistant sheriffs provided to the Prince George’s County Sheriff from four to five. Authorizes the Sheriff to select and appoint the additional assistant sheriff to serve at the Sheriff's pleasure. Substitutes the Fraternal Order of Police for the Deputy Sheriffs’ Association to negotiate benefits other than salary. Updates statutory references governing nonprobationary commissioned employees to current provisions in the Public Safety Article. Requires the county budget to fund the additional assistant sheriff position.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County Office of the Sheriff; Prince George's County Government
qa_results.stakeholders: Prince George's County Sheriff, assistant sheriffs, deputy sheriffs, Fraternal Order of Police, and Prince George's County taxpayers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Prince George's County expenditures increase by approximately $331,600 annually beginning in fiscal 2024 to fund salary and fringe benefits for one additional assistant sheriff. State finances and county revenues are not affected.

qa_results.bill_summary: Increases the authorized speed monitoring systems on Maryland Route 210 in Prince George’s County from three to six. Authorizes the speed monitoring systems to be mobile or stationary. Extends the termination date for placing speed monitoring systems on Maryland Route 210 to September 30, 2028. Requires the State Highway Administration and Prince George’s County Department of Public Works and Transportation to report annually. Mandates reporting on highway accident solutions, distributed fine funds, and planned fund uses beginning December 31, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Highway Administration; Prince George's County Department of Public Works and Transportation
qa_results.stakeholders: Motorists traveling on Maryland Route 210 in Prince George's County; Prince George's County government; State Highway Administration
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Transportation Trust Fund revenues and expenditures increase from FY 2024 through FY 2029 due to additional speed cameras and authorization extension, as net fine revenues are distributed to the State Highway Administration for highway safety improvements. General fund revenues likely increase from contested citations in District Court. Prince George's County experiences no net fiscal impact because local revenue is restricted to cost recovery. Specific total dollar amounts cannot be reliably determined.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDOT SHA is directly responsible for examining safety issues on Maryland Route 210, implementing solutions, receiving net speed camera fine distributions via the Transportation Trust Fund, and submitting an annual findings and funding report to the Governor and General Assembly.

As the parent department of the State Highway Administration, MDOT's Transportation Trust Fund experiences an increase in both revenues and expenditures resulting from the extension and expansion of speed cameras on Route 210.

Under Section 7-302 of the Courts Article referenced in the bill, fines collected from the Route 210 speed cameras are remitted to the Comptroller for distribution to the State Highway Administration.
The District Court, supported by the AOC, will experience an increase in contested speed camera citations and caseloads generated by the additional speed monitoring systems.
The bill mandates that the State Highway Administration submit an annual report detailing findings, safety recommendations, and fund distributions to the Governor.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners to approve the transfer of a Class A license into specified districts. Permits this transfer only if no Class A beer, wine, and liquor license operates within 1 mile of the premises. Authorizes the Board to issue Class B-DD licenses with off-sale privileges to qualifying restaurants outside the Capital Beltway. Repeals the restriction prohibiting the Board from issuing more than six Class B-DD licenses in a designated area. Authorizes up to 50 Class B-DD licenses for restaurants on Central Avenue between the Capital Beltway and the District border. Establishes a $5,000 annual fee for Class B-DD licenses that include off-sale privileges.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Restaurants, alcoholic beverages license holders, and license applicants in Prince George's County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Prince George's County revenues increase beginning in FY 2024 by $3,025 for each standard Class B-DD license issued and by $5,000 for each Class B-DD license with off-sale privileges issued; the total revenue increase is indeterminate. County enforcement costs can be absorbed within existing budgeted resources. No state fiscal effect.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is responsible for regulating the state's alcohol industry. While the bill specifically authorizes local licensing actions taken by the Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners and has no state fiscal impact, it relates to the statutory framework governing alcoholic beverages in the state.

qa_results.bill_summary: Changes the title of the Chief Executive Officer of Prince George's County Public Schools to County Superintendent. Transfers school consolidation and student transportation authority from the superintendent to the county board of education. Establishes the Office of Integrity and Compliance to investigate fraud, waste, and abuse in the local school system. Requires the Prince George's County Council to appoint an Integrity and Compliance Officer to a four-year term. Authorizes the officer to conduct audits, administer oaths, take depositions, and issue subpoenas. Prohibits retaliation against school system employees, vendors, or vendor employees who report violations or assist investigations.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County Council; Prince George's County Board of Education; Office of Integrity and Compliance
qa_results.stakeholders: Prince George's County Public Schools students, personnel, and administration, school system contractors and vendors, and Prince George's County taxpayers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No State fiscal effect. Prince George's County Board of Education expenditures increase by at least $741,041 annually beginning in fiscal 2024 to fund the Integrity and Compliance Officer, a financial administrator, and a financial analyst. Local revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters governance and oversight provisions governing Prince George's County Public Schools, including altering the title and responsibilities of the county superintendent, whose certification and appointment require approval by the State Superintendent of Schools and appointment of search committee members by the State Board of Education.

The bill establishes the Office of Integrity and Compliance in Prince George's County Public Schools and explicitly mandates that the Integrity and Compliance Officer report allegations of serious violations to the State Ethics Commission.
The bill updates statutory provisions relating to the selection process of the Prince George's County Superintendent, which includes members appointed by the Governor to the search committee.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes Class B–Stadium baseball stadium license holders in Prince George’s County to sell liquor alongside beer and wine. Permits sales for on-premises consumption at baseball stadiums owned or operated by the Maryland–National Capital Park and Planning Commission. Allows profits from alcoholic beverage sales to accrue to the Commission or its contracted private concessionaire. Renames the existing football stadium license as the Class B–Stadium football stadium license. Limits the Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners to issuing one baseball stadium license and one football stadium license.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland–National Capital Park and Planning Commission, private concessionaires under contract with the Commission, and patrons at baseball stadiums in Prince George's County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No effect on State finances. Prince George's County finances and operations are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland oversees state alcohol tax collection and regulations across the alcoholic beverage industry. Although this legislation primarily affects Prince George's County local licensing and administration through its Board of License Commissioners, the Comptroller maintains broad state-level regulatory and tax oversight of alcoholic beverage sales.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires a court to set an expedited hearing on a petition regarding a child's proposed relocation. Triggers the expedited hearing requirement for relocations of 40 or more miles from the current primary residence. Requires that the proposed relocation significantly interfere with the other parent's predetermined parenting time schedule. Authorizes either party subject to a custody or visitation order to file the petition. Takes effect October 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary; Circuit Courts
qa_results.stakeholders: Parents and children subject to child custody or visitation orders in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No material effect on State or circuit court finances or operations. Potential minimal expenditures may occur from scheduling expedited hearings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the courts to set expedited hearings on petitions regarding certain proposed relocations of a child in custody or visitation proceedings, directly affecting court scheduling procedures and judicial case management operations.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the governing body of Prince George's County to enter into payment in lieu of taxes agreements. Applies to property used for low-income housing financed through the county's Right of First Refusal program. Covers property acquired, constructed, or rehabilitated to operate rental housing for lower-income persons. Requires property owners to pay a negotiated amount instead of county real property taxes. Mandates maintaining lower-income housing or agreeing to preserve it for at least 5 years.
qa_results.responsible_party: governing body of Prince George's County
qa_results.stakeholders: Owners and developers of qualifying low-income housing developments and lower-income tenants in Prince George's County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No State fiscal effect. Prince George's County property tax revenues may decrease beginning in fiscal 2024 to the extent qualifying properties are exempted, though revenue losses will be mitigated by negotiated PILOT payments. Specific figures are unavailable because impact depends on the number and assessed value of participating developments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill expands local authority in Prince George's County to enter into payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) agreements for low-income and affordable rental housing developments. While the implementation and fiscal impacts are entirely local, the policy directly aligns with the Department of Housing and Community Development's core focus on low-income and affordable rental housing development and financing.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires nonpublic schools educating placed children with disabilities to pay teachers salaries equivalent to local public school salaries. Phases in salary parity over three years beginning in fiscal year 2024. Mandates that the State and counties fund the additional salary costs in the same proportion as placement costs. Prohibits reducing funding for other components of special education placements to fund teacher salaries. Requires the Maryland State Department of Education to adopt implementing regulations.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education
qa_results.stakeholders: teachers at nonpublic special education placement schools, children with disabilities in nonpublic placements, county boards of education, and county governments
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $3.5 million in FY 2024, growing to $11.4 million by FY 2028. County expenditures increase by $5.0 million in FY 2024, growing to $16.3 million by FY 2028.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) is the primary regulatory and implementing agency for the bill. MSDE oversees nonpublic special education placements, calculates and distributes the State share of funding, and is explicitly required to adopt regulations to administer the teacher pay parity requirements.

The bill creates an increasing mandated general fund appropriation for the State share of nonpublic school special education teacher salaries, rising from $3.5 million in FY 2024 to $11.4 million by FY 2028, directly impacting DBM's budget development and fiscal planning duties.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the State Board of Physicians to place a qualifying retired physician on emeritus status. Exempts licensees on inactive status or emeritus status from license expiration terms and continuing medical education requirements. Prohibits licensees on inactive status or emeritus status from practicing medicine, attempting or offering to practice, or delegating medical acts. Authorizes emeritus status licensees to use titles such as doctor or physician without representing authorization to practice medicine. Requires the Board to reinstate the license of an individual on inactive or emeritus status under specified conditions.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Physicians
qa_results.stakeholders: licensed physicians in Maryland who are retired or seeking inactive or emeritus status
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Minimal net impact on State Board of Physicians special fund revenues from status fees. Any additional administrative workload can be handled with existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Board of Physicians is a regulatory board housed within the Maryland Department of Health. The bill directly modifies licensure categories, requirements, and procedures for physicians under the Board's jurisdiction, creating an emeritus status and altering inactive status rules.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits each health occupations board from requiring an applicant to prove lawful presence in the United States. Prohibits each board from requiring a Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number for licensure. Requires each applicant to disclose a Social Security number, an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number, or permitted alternative documentation. Requires each board to record the identification number or alternative documentation in the application file. Authorizes the Child Support Administration to include an obligor's Individual Taxpayer Identification Number in information requests.
qa_results.responsible_party: Health occupations boards; Maryland Department of Health; Child Support Administration; State Department of Assessments and Taxation
qa_results.stakeholders: Applicants for health occupations licenses, certifications, and registrations; immigrant healthcare practitioners; health occupations boards
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund revenues for health occupations boards increase by an indeterminate amount beginning in fiscal 2024 from additional license issuances. Special fund expenditures for the State Board of Nursing increase by up to $100,000 in fiscal 2024 for one-time programming costs, alongside potential additional personnel costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health houses and oversees the state's health occupations boards. The bill directly impacts these boards by prohibiting them from requiring proof of lawful presence or a Social Security number/ITIN as a condition of licensure, modifying application intake processes, and resulting in operational and fiscal impacts on licensing boards (such as the Board of Nursing).

The Department of Human Services oversees the Child Support Administration, which coordinates with professional licensing authorities under the Family Law Article to identify child support obligors in arrears using identification numbers and licensing data.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the authorized use of Purse Dedication Account funds by Ocean Downs Race Course for operating loss assistance. Removes the calendar year 2024 sunset date, making the operating loss assistance permanent. Replaces the $1,200,000 annual limit with an amount equal to up to $30,000 per live racing day held. Requires the assistance to cover operating losses incurred during that calendar year under generally accepted accounting principles. Maintains the requirement to support a minimum of 40 annual live racing days unless prevented by uncontrollable circumstances.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Racing Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Ocean Downs Race Course, standardbred horse owners and trainers, and Maryland standardbred racetracks
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No net effect on State revenues or total special fund expenditures. Purse Dedication Account funds are redirected to Ocean Downs Race Course, increasing its allocation by approximately $210,000 annually in calendar 2023 and 2024 and by roughly $1.41 million annually thereafter, correspondingly reducing funds available for standardbred track purses.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Racing Commission, which administers and holds statutory authority over the Purse Dedication Account and allocates funds to horse racing venues, is housed within the Department of Labor.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency regulates commercial gaming and video lottery terminals in Maryland, the proceeds of which directly fund the Purse Dedication Account.
The Comptroller is responsible for the collection and distribution of state revenues and special fund allocations, including distributions derived from video lottery terminal proceeds.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the State Board of Pharmacy to adopt regulations ensuring accessible prescription labels, bag tags, and medical guides. Guarantees access at no additional cost to individuals who are blind, visually impaired, or otherwise print disabled. Directs the Board to allow visually impaired individuals an opportunity to provide input on the regulations. Mandates that the Board adopt the regulations on or before January 1, 2025. Requires the Maryland Department of Health to report on potential enhanced dispensing fees by December 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Pharmacy; Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: individuals who are blind, visually impaired, or otherwise print disabled; pharmacies
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The State Board of Pharmacy and the Maryland Department of Health can implement the bill using existing budgeted resources. There is no effect on local government finances. Small business pharmacies may incur additional compliance costs depending on the regulations adopted by the Board.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly requires the State Board of Pharmacy (housed within MDH) to adopt regulations ensuring accessible prescription labels for blind, visually impaired, or print-disabled individuals, and requires MDH to submit a report to the General Assembly evaluating the costs and process of implementing enhanced dispensing fees.

The bill establishes accessibility requirements for individuals who are blind, visually impaired, or otherwise print disabled, which aligns with the Department of Disabilities' mandate to coordinate accessible services and advocate for accommodations across state programs and healthcare settings.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Interagency Commission on School Construction as an independent unit of State government. Repeals the School Safety Grant Program and the Aging Schools Program effective June 30, 2026. Raises project cost thresholds requiring State Superintendent approval for school building remodeling and change orders. Requires county boards of education to evaluate 50-year life cycle costs and alternative energy systems during design development. Increases annual statutory transfers to Prince George's County public-private partnership school construction to $27,000,000 starting in fiscal 2025.
qa_results.responsible_party: Interagency Commission on School Construction; Maryland State Department of Education; Maryland Stadium Authority; Department of General Services
qa_results.stakeholders: local school boards; Prince George's County Board of Education; public school students and educators
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $123,300 in FY 2024 for an Interagency Commission human resources administrator, and by approximately $2.1 million annually beginning in FY 2025 to backfill $2.0 million in Education Trust Fund revenues redirected to the Prince George's County public-private partnership. Beginning in FY 2027, $16.1 million formerly mandated for the Aging Schools and School Safety Grant programs is assumed redirected to the Nancy K. Kopp Public School Facilities Priority Fund. Prince George's County Public Schools revenues increase by $2.0 million annually starting in FY 2025.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 458 establishes the Interagency Commission on School Construction (IAC) as an independent unit of State government, alters member removal provisions, repeals certain grant programs under its purview, assigns it administration of the Prince George's County P3 Fund, and requires it to develop life cycle cost analysis standards and submit annual reports.

The bill formally separates the IAC from functioning within the Maryland State Department of Education, alters approval thresholds for school construction and remodeling for the State Superintendent of Schools, and requires coordination on life cycle cost analysis standards.

The bill alters funding streams managed by the Authority under the Built to Learn Program, increases its required transfers from the Supplemental Public School Construction Financing Fund to the Prince George's County P3 Fund to $27 million annually, and requires joint progress reporting.

The bill explicitly requires the Department of General Services to coordinate with the IAC and the State Department of Education to develop life cycle cost analysis standards. In addition, the Secretary of General Services serves as an ex officio member of the IAC.

The bill removes the requirement that the Board of Public Works approve grants awarded by the IAC under the Capital Grant Program for Local School Systems With Significant Enrollment Growth or Relocatable Classrooms.

The Comptroller is mandated to deposit specified amounts from the Education Trust Fund into the Supplemental Public School Construction Financing Fund and is responsible for accounting for the Prince George's County Public–Private Partnership Fund.

The State Treasurer is required to hold, manage, and invest the monies of both the Prince George's County Public–Private Partnership Fund and the Supplemental Public School Construction Financing Fund.

The Governor retains appointment and removal powers over appointed members of the newly independent IAC, jointly selects the commission chair, receives annual evaluations and reports regarding P3 agreements, and is authorized to process a budget amendment transferring $25 million.
The Secretary of Planning (or designee) serves as a statutory member of the Interagency Commission on School Construction.

The bill impacts state budget allocations, requiring adjustments to the general fund to backfill revenue shifted from the Education Trust Fund, and involves personnel and budget adjustments associated with establishing IAC as an independent agency.

qa_results.bill_summary: Continues the State Board of Architects in accordance with the Maryland Program Evaluation Act. Extends the termination date for the board's statutory and regulatory authority to July 1, 2028. Maintains the licensing and regulation of individual architects in the State. Preserves the board's authority to issue licenses, permits, and disciplinary penalties. Takes effect June 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Architects; Maryland Department of Labor
qa_results.stakeholders: Licensed architects, architectural business permit holders, applicants for architectural licensure, and consumers of architectural services in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund revenues and expenditures for the State Board of Architects are maintained through fiscal 2028. No local fiscal effect.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Architects is housed within the Maryland Department of Labor's Division of Occupational and Professional Licensing. The bill extends the termination date of the Board to July 1, 2028, directly allowing the Department to continue licensing and regulating architects and maintaining related special fund revenues and expenditures.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes an individual under the age of 16 years to use specified gear without a recreational crabbing license. Applies to catching or attempting to catch crabs in the waters of the Chesapeake Bay and its tidal tributaries. Permits the youth to use a collapsible trap, net ring, handline, or dip net. Requires the authorized gear to match descriptions established by the Department of Natural Resources in regulations. Takes effect June 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources
qa_results.stakeholders: individuals under the age of 16 years catching crabs recreationally in the Chesapeake Bay and its tidal tributaries
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not materially affected, with any potential decrease in recreational crabbing license fee revenues expected to be negligible. There is no local government fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Natural Resources Article to allow individuals under 16 years of age to use specified recreational crabbing gear in the Chesapeake Bay and its tidal tributaries without a license, as described by the Department in regulations. The Department of Natural Resources manages the state's fisheries, recreational crabbing licensing, and related regulations.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Department of Natural Resources to permit Sunday hunting of game birds and mammals in Worcester County. Allows this hunting on private property and designated public land during open seasons. Restricts Sunday hunting hours generally from 30 minutes before sunrise until 10:30 a.m. Lifts the morning time restriction during deer firearms season and designated deer bow hunting Sundays. Reduces the archery hunting safety zone around occupied buildings in Worcester County from 150 yards to 50 yards.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources
qa_results.stakeholders: Hunters, landowners, and outdoor-related businesses in Worcester County
