Caps subscription rates for low- and moderate-income subscribers at 90% of the bill credit value. Mandates prevailing wage rates on projects exceeding one megawatt unless subject to a project labor agreement. Extends the personal property tax exemption application window for qualifying community solar systems.
qa_results.responsible_party: Public Service Commission; State Department of Assessments and Taxation
qa_results.stakeholders: community solar developers, subscriber organizations, subscription coordinators, electric companies, electric utility ratepayers, and low- and moderate-income subscribers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund expenditures and revenues for the Public Service Commission increase by $264,900 in FY 2024, reflecting staffing and consultant costs funded by assessments on public service companies. Local personal property tax revenues potentially decrease beginning in FY 2026 due to the extended application window for community solar exemptions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary regulatory and implementing agency for the Community Solar Energy Generating Systems Program. The bill mandates PSC to make the program permanent, adopt comprehensive revised and new regulations, approve electric company tariffs, establish a stakeholder workgroup, and create a new full-time position dedicated to administering the program.

OPC represents residential utility consumers before the PSC. The bill establishes new billing structures, rate limitations, consumer protections, and low- to moderate-income provisions that directly affect residential utility customers and require PSC proceedings in which OPC participates.

The bill requires developers of community solar systems with a capacity exceeding 1 megawatt to pay workers at least the prevailing wage rate determined under Title 17, Subtitle 2 of the State Finance and Procurement Article, which is established and administered by the Maryland Department of Labor.
The bill defines and incorporates 'agrivoltaics' into project siting and co-location standards, referencing agricultural activities recognized by the Maryland Department of Agriculture.

The bill requires community solar energy generating system developers to address critical area, climate resilience, and forest conservation concerns by complying with the Forest Conservation Act and Critical Area requirements overseen by DNR.

qa_results.bill_summary: Continues the State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors until July 1, 2026. Requires the Maryland Department of Labor to hire a consultant to evaluate the Commission. Assesses Commission adherence to diversity, equity, and inclusion guidelines under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice. Requires conducting the evaluation in consultation with the Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability. Directs the Department to submit the evaluation report to designated legislative committees by January 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor; State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors; Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability
qa_results.stakeholders: Licensed real estate appraisers, appraisal management companies, and home inspectors in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund expenditures increase by between $50,000 and $75,000 in FY 2024 for the Maryland Department of Labor to hire an independent consultant. Commission special fund revenues and expenditures are otherwise maintained from FY 2024 through FY 2026. No local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors is housed within the Maryland Department of Labor. The bill extends the Commission's termination date to July 1, 2026, and requires the Department to hire an independent consultant to evaluate the Commission's adherence to diversity, equity, and inclusion guidelines, resulting in special fund expenditures of $50,000 to $75,000 in FY 2024.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly extends the statutory and regulatory authority and termination date of an ongoing state regulatory commission—the State Commission of Real Estate Appraisers, Appraisal Management Companies, and Home Inspectors—through July 1, 2026, and mandates an independent evaluation of its regulatory practices.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Public Service Commission to establish targets for deploying new energy storage devices in the State. Sets cumulative capacity goals of 750 megawatts by 2027, 1,500 megawatts by 2030, and 3,000 megawatts by 2033. Requires reducing any target that cannot be met cost-effectively to the maximum cost-effective deployable amount. Establishes the Maryland Energy Storage Program and mandates its implementation by July 1, 2025. Mandates competitive procurement mechanisms and authorizes energy storage credits and utility contracting requirements.
qa_results.responsible_party: Public Service Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: investor-owned electric companies, electric customers and ratepayers, and energy storage project developers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund expenditures for the Public Service Commission increase by $649,600 in FY 2025 to hire six staff, fully offset by assessments on public service companies. State and local government expenditures on electricity likely increase beginning as early as FY 2025.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary implementing agency responsible for establishing deployment targets, administering and implementing the Maryland Energy Storage Program, conducting rulemakings, and reporting to the General Assembly.

The Office of the People's Counsel represents residential utility consumers in Public Service Commission proceedings, which will include the proceedings, rulemakings, and rate recovery mechanisms associated with the deployment of energy storage systems and related ratepayer impacts.

The Maryland Energy Administration coordinates state energy policy and renewable energy initiatives, and collaborates on statewide energy storage planning and oversight connected to existing pilot storage programs.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires student financing companies to register annually with the Commissioner of Financial Regulation starting March 15, 2024. Mandates annual reporting of detailed loan volume, default rates, and terms for Maryland borrowers by March 15 each year. Directs the Commissioner to publish reported information on a publicly accessible website by June 15 each year. Renders student financing products void and unenforceable if a company knowingly violates registration or reporting mandates. Authorizes the Commissioner, the Attorney General, and county State's Attorneys to enforce these requirements. Permits the Commissioner to bar individuals from student financing roles for up to 10 years for harmful violations.
qa_results.responsible_party: Commissioner of Financial Regulation in the Maryland Department of Labor; Office of the Attorney General
qa_results.stakeholders: Student financing companies, institutions of postsecondary education offering student financing, and Maryland consumers obtaining or holding student financing products
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No material effect on State finances, as the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation can implement the bill with existing resources and registration fees are paid to a third-party licensing system. Local government finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Commissioner of Financial Regulation, housed within the Maryland Department of Labor, with registering student financing companies, receiving annual reports, creating and maintaining a public database, establishing regulations, and conducting investigations and enforcement.

The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General, alongside the Commissioner of Financial Regulation and local State's Attorneys, to enforce the requirements and exercise investigative and enforcement powers under the subtitle.

The bill makes certain noncompliant student financing contracts void and unenforceable in legal actions and references court enforcement of investigative subpoenas, potentially impacting judicial proceedings and court filings.

qa_results.bill_summary: Clarifies venue requirements for judicial review of a final decision or order of the Public Service Commission. Requires a proceeding to be instituted in the Circuit Court for Baltimore City or an authorized county circuit court. Restricts county venue to any county where the public service company that was a party provides service. Removes obsolete statutory references to circuit courts in equity. Takes effect October 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Public Service Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Public service companies, parties to Public Service Commission proceedings, and litigants seeking judicial review of Commission decisions
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local finances or operations. Administrative expenditures for the Public Service Commission may decrease or be reallocated due to reduced travel for legal staff from limited judicial review venues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies the statutory venue provisions governing where proceedings for judicial review of the Public Service Commission's final decisions and orders must be filed, potentially reducing travel and administrative expenditures for PSC legal staff.

The Office of the People's Counsel frequently represents residential utility consumers in proceedings before the PSC and routinely exercises its statutory authority under § 3-202 to seek judicial review of PSC decisions, meaning this venue limitation directly applies to their appeals.
The bill alters the jurisdictional venue rules determining which county circuit courts or the Circuit Court for Baltimore City may hear judicial reviews of PSC decisions.
The Secretary of the Environment has specific statutory authority under § 3-202 to seek judicial review of PSC orders, which are governed by the venue provisions amended by this bill.

The Secretary of Natural Resources has specific statutory authority under § 3-202 to seek judicial review of PSC decisions regarding power plant siting, and any such proceedings are subject to the venue requirements set by this bill.
Section 3-202 specifically references actions where the Motor Vehicle Administration suspends or revokes vehicle carrier registrations pursuant to an order of the PSC.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City to offer a monetary compromise in lieu of a hearing. Requires agreeing license holders to waive hearing rights, admit alleged facts, take prescribed corrective action, and accept the penalty. Directs the Board to maintain records, make safety findings, state accepted compromises on record, and publicly post decisions. Requires the Board to adopt regulations to implement the compromise process. Increases the maximum fine from $3,000 to $20,000 for subsequent offenses causing license suspension. Increases the maximum fine from $3,000 to $20,000 for unauthorized pub crawl promoter violations.
qa_results.responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City
qa_results.stakeholders: alcoholic beverages license holders and pub crawl promoters in Baltimore City
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Potential increase in Baltimore City revenues from monetary penalties collected via offers of compromise and higher maximum fines. Procedural requirements can be handled with existing Baltimore City resources, and there is no State fiscal effect.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners to approve specified license expansions and issuances in the 46th district. Permits qualifying Class D beer and light wine license holders to convert licenses upon paying a $15,000 fee. Authorizes new Class B beer, wine, and liquor licenses for restaurants meeting specific investment standards. Alters seating capacity limits for license transfers within ward 3, precinct 3 to fewer than 200 individuals. Extends the expiration of specified licenses until July 1, 2024, to complete transfers or renewals.
qa_results.responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore City
qa_results.stakeholders: alcoholic beverages licensees, restaurant owners, and applicants in Baltimore City's 46th alcoholic beverages district
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Minimal increase in Baltimore City revenues beginning in FY 2024 from additional license issuances, conversions, and transfer fees. No state fiscal effect.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is responsible for collecting state alcohol and sales taxes and regulates the alcohol industry at the state level. While this bill specifically alters local retail alcoholic beverage licenses administered by the Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners, it pertains to the broader regulation and taxation of alcoholic beverages.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes consumer protections for motor vehicle glass repair or replacement on vehicles with advanced driver assistance systems. Requires motor vehicle safety glass facilities to inform customers if system recalibration is required before glass work. Requires facilities to provide a written statement that work will meet or exceed original equipment manufacturer specifications. Prohibits facilities from charging for services that are not performed or successfully completed. Requires facilities to inform customers if required recalibration is not performed or successfully completed. Makes violations an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
qa_results.responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
qa_results.stakeholders: Motor vehicle owners with vehicles equipped with advanced driver assistance systems; motor vehicle safety glass facilities
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No material impact on State or local finances or operations. The Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division, can handle the bill's requirements with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes that violations by motor vehicle safety glass facilities are unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, which is directly enforced and investigated by the Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division.

The bill references definitions in the Transportation Article and relates to motor vehicle safety systems; MDOT was consulted as an information source for the legislation, though it has no direct regulatory or enforcement mandate under the bill.

While the bill amends the Commercial Law Article, motor vehicle safety glass repairs and ADAS recalibrations commonly involve auto insurance claims, leading to MIA being consulted as an information source.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits the Department of Commerce from denying economic development program benefits solely because an applicant is a licensed cannabis establishment. Applies this prohibition to programs under Title 5 of the Economic Development Article and the More Jobs for Marylanders Program. Requires the cannabis business entity to otherwise satisfy all program requirements, including industry sector-specific criteria. Authorizes cannabis establishments previously denied benefits or certification before July 1, 2023, solely on that basis to reapply. Adds the growth, processing, or dispensing of cannabis as eligible activities for Job Creation and One Maryland tax credits.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Commerce
qa_results.stakeholders: licensed cannabis business entities, including medical cannabis growers, processors, and dispensaries
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues decrease, potentially significantly, beginning in FY 2025 as newly eligible cannabis dispensaries claim Job Creation and One Maryland tax credits, largely driven by uncapped One Maryland credits. Transportation Trust Fund and Higher Education Investment Fund revenues, as well as local highway user revenues, decrease to the extent credits are claimed against the corporate income tax.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Commerce is the primary implementing agency tasked with administering Title 5 economic development programs, certifying entities for the More Jobs for Marylanders Program, and administering the Job Creation and One Maryland tax credits to include licensed cannabis establishments.

The Comptroller of Maryland administers the state tax system, including processing and auditing the Job Creation and One Maryland tax credits claimed on income tax returns, which are expected to decrease general fund and special fund revenues.

The Maryland Cannabis Administration licenses and regulates the cannabis growers, processors, dispensaries, and other cannabis establishments that are granted eligibility for state economic development benefits and tax credits under the bill.
The Department of Transportation is minimally affected via a potential decrease in Transportation Trust Fund revenues resulting from tax credits claimed against the corporate income tax.

qa_results.bill_summary: Provides that the Governor appoints the Secretary of Higher Education to serve at the Governor's pleasure. Requires each public institution of higher education to adopt a written policy providing reasonable academic accommodations for religious beliefs. Requires each public institution of higher education, except University of Maryland Global Campus, to provide campus space for religious practices. Alters eligibility criteria for the Guaranteed Access Grant and the Next Generation Scholars of Maryland Program. Transfers the administration and awarding of Maryland Community College Promise Scholarships from state financial aid staff to community colleges. Repeals statutory intent to reorganize the Office of Student Financial Assistance as a separate independent agency.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission; Office of Student Financial Assistance; Governor; Maryland State Department of Education
qa_results.stakeholders: higher education students, public institutions of higher education, community colleges, and students observing religious beliefs
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $278,200 in FY 2024 for contractual modifications to the Maryland College Aid Processing System. Baltimore City Community College and locally funded community colleges incur administrative expenditures beginning in FY 2024 to verify eligibility and award Promise Scholarships. Beginning in FY 2026, institutions incur administrative costs to process Guaranteed Access Grants, potentially offset by state funding. The State avoids indeterminate operational costs by repealing the planned independent agency spin-off of the Office of Student Financial Assistance.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHEC is the primary regulatory agency impacted by the bill. The legislation alters the appointment and reporting structure of the Secretary of Higher Education, reforms the Delegate Howard P. Rawlings Educational Excellence Awards (EEA) and Guaranteed Access (GA) Grants, restructures the Maryland Community College Promise Scholarship administration, and repeals the planned spin-off of the Office of Student Financial Assistance (OSFA).

As the state's postsecondary coordinating board and administrator of state financial assistance, MHEC is directly responsible for implementing the financial aid reforms, auditing community college awards, and working with advisory councils on regulatory implementation.

The bill directly modifies the Governor's appointment power by removing the requirement to select the Secretary of Higher Education from a list of MHEC nominees and establishing that the Secretary serves at the pleasure of the Governor. It also expresses legislative intent regarding gubernatorial budget requests for financial aid administration funding.

USM institutions are public institutions of higher education that must adopt written religious accommodation policies, provide campus spaces for religious practices (with an exemption for UMGC), and implement new responsibilities for notifying students of Guaranteed Access Grant awards and calculating financial aid packages.

As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State University is required to establish religious accommodation policies and campus spaces, as well as take on financial aid notification and administration duties for the Guaranteed Access Grant program.

As a public four-year institution, St. Mary's College of Maryland must adopt faith-based academic accommodation policies, designate space on campus for religious practices, and administer Guaranteed Access Grant notifications and packaging for its students.

MSDE administers the Next Generation Scholars of Maryland Program in collaboration with MHEC. The bill alters student eligibility criteria for the program to include students who qualify for free or reduced-price lunch and allows continued participation for students who move to nonparticipating counties.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters Sunday hours of sale for specified alcoholic beverages licenses in Frederick County. Authorizes special Sunday opening permit holders for Class A licenses to sell starting at 6 a.m. Expands Sunday sales hours for Class B and Class C license holders to run from 6 a.m. to 2 a.m. Repeals prohibitions against Class B licensees selling alcoholic beverages at a bar or counter on Sunday. Aligns Sunday sales hours for conference centers, dinner theaters, entertainment centers, hotel lobbies, and municipal golf courses.
qa_results.responsible_party: Frederick County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: holders of specified alcoholic beverages licenses in Frederick County and retail alcohol consumers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state fiscal effect. The bill does not materially affect Frederick County finances or operations, though small business license holders may realize increased sales revenue from expanded Sunday operating hours.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller regulates Maryland's alcohol industry and issues state-level alcohol licenses referenced in related provisions (such as Class 7 micro-brewery licenses), although retail sales hours in Frederick County are administered primarily at the local level.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners to issue up to five Class B–DD (Development District) licenses. Restricts eligibility to restaurants located within the Main Street Laurel development area. Defines the geographic boundaries from northbound Washington Boulevard to 7th Street, between the Patuxent River and Prince George Street. Permits license holders to sell beer, wine, and liquor for on-premises consumption seven days per week. Takes effect July 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Restaurants located within the Main Street Laurel development area in Prince George's County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Prince George's County revenues increase by $3,025 annually for each Class B-DD license issued, though the total number of licenses that will be issued cannot be reliably estimated. County enforcement can be handled with existing budgeted resources. There is no state fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is responsible for regulating aspects of the alcoholic beverages industry and collecting state alcohol excise and sales taxes. While this bill specifically authorizes the local Prince George's County Board of License Commissioners to issue local retail licenses with no direct state fiscal impact, it relates to the regulation of alcoholic beverages within the state.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the governing body of Charles County to grant a property tax credit against county property taxes. Applies to real property owned and occupied as the principal residence of an emergency responder or unmarried surviving spouse. Limits eligibility to individuals with a federal adjusted gross income of $150,000 or less for the preceding taxable year. Defines an emergency responder as an active or retired volunteer member of a Charles County fire, rescue, or emergency medical services company. Allows the county to determine the credit amount, duration, and additional eligibility criteria.
qa_results.responsible_party: Governing Body of Charles County
qa_results.stakeholders: Active and retired volunteer members of fire, rescue, and emergency medical services companies in Charles County and their unmarried surviving spouses
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Charles County property tax revenues decrease by $347,300 in FY 2024 and $375,900 in FY 2028 if the tax credit is granted. County expenditures increase by $115,900 in FY 2024 and $130,400 in FY 2028 for administrative staff in the County Treasurer's Office. No state fiscal effect.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill authorizes Charles County to grant a local property tax credit on the principal residence of volunteer emergency responders. Although the credit is established and administered locally by Charles County with no state fiscal effect, the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board (through its local board in Charles County) serves as the appellate administrative body for disputes concerning property valuations, exemptions, and tax credits.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Maryland Native Plants Program to promote the use and sale of Maryland native plants. Requires the Maryland Department of Agriculture to administer the program and establish a voluntary certification program. Requires the University of Maryland Extension to hire a native plant specialist to direct educational components. Directs the Department to maintain a commercial native plant list and a Maryland Natives marketing program. Mandates annual state budget appropriations of $150,000 for the Extension and $100,000 for the Department starting in fiscal 2025.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Agriculture; University of Maryland Extension; Department of Natural Resources
qa_results.stakeholders: Commercial plant growers, retail nurseries, wholesale nurseries, garden centers, landscapers, and plant consumers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $285,100 in fiscal 2025 and ongoing years for personnel and operating costs. The bill mandates annual appropriations starting in fiscal 2025 of $150,000 for the University of Maryland Extension and $100,000 for the Maryland Department of Agriculture. Local government finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDA is the primary agency responsible for administering the Maryland Native Plants Program, including establishing a voluntary certification program for growers and retailers, developing the Commercial Maryland Native Plant List, operating the 'Maryland Natives' marketing program, and receiving a mandated annual appropriation of $100,000 to hire staff.

The University of Maryland Extension, an entity of USM, is tasked with co-administering the program, administering all educational components, creating and maintaining the 'Maryland Native Plants' webpage, and hiring an extension agent as a native plant specialist supported by a mandated annual appropriation of $150,000.

DNR is required to provide input into the creation and triennial update of the Commercial Maryland Native Plant List and cultivar evaluations, and must host a link to the program's webpage on its native plants website.
The bill mandates that the Governor include specific annual budget appropriations starting in FY 2025 of $150,000 for UME and $100,000 for MDA in the annual state budget.
DBM oversees the preparation and execution of the state budget and manages state personnel, requiring it to incorporate the bill's mandated funding and accommodate the new state positions.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits the State Department of Assessments and Taxation from disbursing funds to any county that fails to provide required tax sale information. Alters the reporting period for county tax sale data to the second immediately preceding taxable year. Restricts homeowner-specific data collection to properties offered for sale, sold, or subject to foreclosure. Requires each county conducting tax sales to submit all specified information on department forms. Applies the funding prohibition prospectively to surveys conducted on or after June 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland counties conducting tax sales and property owners subject to tax sales
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State and local finances are not anticipated to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Administrative Office of the Courts collaborates with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation and counties to provide data regarding properties for which the right of redemption has been foreclosed by private certificate holders, making it relevant to the data collection process addressed in the bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Governor annually to proclaim October 5 as Dashain Day. Recognizes Dashain as a festival originating in Nepal that celebrates and symbolizes the victory of good over evil. Renumbers existing sections of the General Provisions Article to accommodate the new commemoration. Takes effect October 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Governor
qa_results.stakeholders: Nepalese and South Asian communities in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State and local finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly requires the Governor to annually issue a proclamation declaring October 5 as Dashain Day.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Public Service Commission to employ cybersecurity experts to advise commissioners and support public service companies. Requires the Commission to collaborate with the Office of Security Management to establish cybersecurity standards and best practices. Requires public service companies, excluding common carriers and telephone companies, to adopt zero-trust cybersecurity approaches. Requires affected public service companies to engage third parties for biennial cybersecurity assessments beginning July 1, 2024. Requires public service companies to report cybersecurity incidents to the State Security Operations Center. Requires the Commission to submit biennial cybersecurity reports to the State Chief Information Security Officer beginning January 1, 2025.
qa_results.responsible_party: Public Service Commission; Department of Information Technology; Office of Security Management; State Security Operations Center; State Chief Information Security Officer
qa_results.stakeholders: Regulated public service companies, including investor-owned electric companies, electric cooperatives, municipal electric utilities, gas companies, and water companies (excluding common carriers and telephone companies), and Maryland utility customers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund expenditures and offsetting revenues for the Public Service Commission increase by $364,400 in FY 2024 (and $446,200 in FY 2025) for three new staff positions funded through utility assessments. Local expenditures for municipal electric utilities increase by an indeterminate amount beginning in FY 2024 for biennial third-party assessments. The Department of Information Technology can implement requirements with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 969 directly impacts the Public Service Commission (PSC) by requiring it to hire dedicated cybersecurity experts, collaborate on cybersecurity standards and best practices for regulated utilities, collect biennial compliance certifications, and submit biennial reports on utility cybersecurity posture to the State Chief Information Security Officer.

The bill assigns substantial responsibilities to DoIT and its units, including the Office of Security Management (OSM), the State Chief Information Security Officer (SCISO), and the State Security Operations Center. DoIT collaborates with the PSC to establish standards, establishes incident reporting processes for public service companies, receives incident notifications, and is authorized to receive transferred Dedicated Purpose Account funds for cybersecurity staffing and operational capacity.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation to study mold assessment and remediation practices. Directs the workgroup to examine standards from specified industry organizations, state governments, international governments, and federal guidelines. Requires the workgroup to assess the extent to which climate change increases indoor mold development. Mandates recommending best practices for identifying, preventing, and remediating indoor mold harmful to public health. Requires the workgroup to report findings and recommendations to the Governor and the General Assembly by October 1, 2024.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment; Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland residents, building occupants, property owners, and mold assessment and remediation professionals
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures are minimally affected as workgroup expense reimbursements and staffing costs are absorbable within existing Maryland Department of the Environment resources. There is no effect on revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of the Environment or designee serves as the chair of the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation, and the department is responsible for providing staff support and designating an accreditation representative.
The Secretary of General Services or designee is designated by statute as a member of the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation.
The Secretary of Health or designee is designated by statute as a member of the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation to evaluate health impacts and remediation standards.
The Secretary of Housing and Community Development or designee is designated as a member of the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation.
The Secretary of Labor or designee is designated as a member of the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill formally establishes a new temporary advisory body, the Workgroup on Mold Standards and Remediation, to conduct a study and issue recommendations.
The Workgroup is statutorily mandated to submit its findings and recommended best practices to the Governor on or before October 1, 2024.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner as a unit within the Maryland Department of Health. Redesignates the State Postmortem Examiners Commission as the Postmortem Examiners Advisory Committee. Authorizes the Maryland Department of Health to employ contractual physicians on a per diem basis. Prohibits the Department and the Advisory Committee from interfering with clinical autopsy findings and conclusions. Exempts certain reemployed Employees' Pension System retirees serving as health care practitioners from pension benefit offsets.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health; Office of the Chief Medical Examiner; Postmortem Examiners Advisory Committee
qa_results.stakeholders: reemployed Employees' Pension System retirees serving as contractual health care practitioners, medical examiners and forensic staff, county medical societies, and the Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No material effect on State or local finances or pension liabilities and contribution rates, as changes are primarily procedural.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly establishes the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner as a unit within the Department of Health, transfers administrative and staffing powers from the former commission to the Department and the Secretary of Health, and authorizes MDH to adopt rules and hire contract/per diem physicians.

The bill amends the State Personnel and Pensions Article to exempt Employees' Pension System retirees who are reemployed contractually by MDH as health care practitioners in the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner from standard retirement allowance reductions.
The bill requires the Department of Health to set compensation for designated medical examiner and forensic personnel with the approval of the Secretary of Budget and Management.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes and defines the duties of the Postmortem Examiners Advisory Committee, which advises the Secretary of Health and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

The Secretary of State Police is designated by statute as an ex officio member of the Postmortem Examiners Advisory Committee, and State Police collaborate closely on medical examiner death investigations.
The head of the Pathology Department of the University of Maryland School of Medicine is designated by statute as a member of the Postmortem Examiners Advisory Committee.

The bill references and maintains the role of the Office of Administrative Hearings to conduct contested case hearings and submit findings of fact when an individual appeals a denial by the Chief Medical Examiner to correct autopsy findings.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a human services career pilot program and companion scholarship in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, and Prince George's County. Expands the police officer loan assistance repayment and scholarship programs to include parole and probation agents. Mandates annual budget appropriations of $5,000,000 each for the loan repayment and scholarship programs. Requires the State to match employee supplemental retirement contributions up to $600 per fiscal year. Authorizes an equivalent retirement match up to $600 for employees documenting higher education student loan payments.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Human Services; Maryland Higher Education Commission; Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services; State Board of Trustees of the Maryland Teachers and State Employees Supplemental Retirement Plans
qa_results.stakeholders: State employees participating in supplemental retirement plans, parole and probation agents in the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, public school students and staff in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, and Prince George's County, and Department of Human Services employees
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures increase by $21.8 million in FY 2024 ($13.5 million general funds, $4.1 million special funds, and $4.1 million federal funds) and by $21.7 million annually thereafter, driven primarily by State supplemental retirement matching contributions and new scholarships. Mandated annual appropriations shift $3.5 million from the police scholarship program to the loan assistance repayment program. Local school system expenditures in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, and Prince George's County may increase to adjust required curricula.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates the Pilot Program for Human Services Careers within the Department of Human Services (DHS), requiring DHS to collaborate with local school systems, prioritize program participants in hiring, pay stipends, assign and compensate employee mentors, and partner with MHEC to select scholarship recipients.

MHEC is responsible for administering the newly established Pilot Program for Human Services Careers Scholarship and administering the expanded Maryland Loan Assistance Repayment Program and Scholarship Program for Police Officers and Probation Agents, requiring system updates to MDCAPS and additional personnel.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Teachers & State Employees Supplemental Retirement Plans
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates State matching contributions of up to $600 per fiscal year for participating employees in State supplemental retirement plans (including matches for higher education student loan repayments), increasing total assets under management and fee revenues for MSRP.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly benefits DPSCS by expanding eligibility for the Maryland Loan Assistance Repayment Program and the Maryland Police Officers Scholarship Program to include DPSCS parole and probation agents, supervisors, and regional administrators.

As the State's central personnel and budget agency, DBM is responsible for statewide personnel benefits, coordinating the implementation of the State supplemental retirement matching contributions across State agencies, and incorporating mandated appropriations in the state budget.

The bill requires local school systems to collaborate with DHS to identify students, create internships, add human services career competencies to curriculum, and integrate career opportunities into middle and high school career counseling programs under education law.

USM institutions serve as eligible public senior higher education institutions where scholarship recipients and participants in the police/probation and human services career programs will enroll and use state tuition assistance funds.

The bill establishes statutory mandated annual budget appropriations that the Governor must include in the annual state budget bill ($5,000,000 for the loan assistance repayment program and $5,000,000 for the scholarship program).

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Wildlife Conservation, Education, and Outreach Program within the Department of Natural Resources to promote outdoor recreation and stewardship. Increases statutory fees for multiple hunting and trapping licenses, stamps, and permits, and codifies furbearer permit fees. Creates new resident and nonresident sika deer hunting stamps. Authorizes nonresident students attending a Maryland college or university to purchase a resident hunting license with proof of enrollment. Expands the Heritage Conservation Fund to include acquiring land usable by the general public for hunting. Requires the Department of Natural Resources, in consultation with the Department of Agriculture, to develop a deer overpopulation plan.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources; Maryland Department of Agriculture
qa_results.stakeholders: hunters, trappers, nonresident college students attending Maryland institutions, farmers, and private landowners
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund revenues and expenditures increase by an estimated $2,271,600 annually beginning in fiscal 2024 due to increased license, stamp, and permit fees. Federal grant matching revenues increase by an estimated $6,814,900 annually beginning in fiscal 2025, which will fund staff and a farmer cost-share program. No direct local government fiscal effect.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DNR is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill, including establishing the Wildlife Conservation, Education, and Outreach Program, administering altered and new hunting/trapping license and stamp fees, managing the Heritage Conservation Fund and Wildlife Management and Protection Fund, creating eight new staff positions, and developing a statewide deer overpopulation plan.

DNR is required to consult with the Department of Agriculture to develop a plan addressing the overpopulation of deer in Maryland, and the bill establishes a farmer cost-share program to plant forage crops on agricultural land.
The bill mandates the creation of eight new Position Identification Numbers (PINs) for department personnel and involves significant ongoing state special and federal fund budgetary adjustments.
The bill codifies that the balance of migratory game bird stamp fees is paid over and accounted to the State Treasurer to be credited to the State Wildlife Management and Protection Fund.

qa_results.bill_summary: Consolidates collective bargaining laws for State employees, public school employees, and community college employees into the State Government Article. Establishes the Public Employee Relations Board as an independent State agency to oversee collective bargaining activities. Repeals the State Labor Relations Board, State Higher Education Labor Relations Board, and Public School Labor Relations Board. Requires certification of an exclusive representative without an election if a petition is supported by a majority of unit employees. Prohibits public employers from engaging in lockouts and prohibits public employees from engaging in strikes.
qa_results.responsible_party: Public Employee Relations Board
qa_results.stakeholders: State employees, public school employees, community college employees, public employers, and public employee labor organizations
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least $642,600 in FY 2024 to fund board member compensation, three deputy directors, legal counsel, and operational start-up costs for the new board, rising to $888,400 by FY 2028. Local expenditures are not anticipated to be materially affected, and revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 984 establishes the Public Employee Relations Board (PERB) as an independent state agency responsible for overseeing and administering collective bargaining, union elections, and unfair labor practice disputes across Maryland public employers.

agency_relevance.agency_name: State Higher Education Labor Relations Board
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly repeals the State Higher Education Labor Relations Board and consolidates its responsibilities, functions, and pending matters into the newly established PERB.
The bill explicitly repeals the Public School Labor Relations Board and consolidates its powers, duties, and pending matters into the newly established PERB.

As the State's central personnel agency, DBM represents the State in collective bargaining negotiations under Title 3 of the State Personnel and Pensions Article, which is heavily amended and standardized under the bill.
The bill substantially modifies and restructures the statutory provisions in the Education Article governing collective bargaining for certificated and noncertificated public school personnel.
The bill explicitly authorizes hearings on unfair labor practice complaints to be conducted before the Office of Administrative Hearings.
The bill sets requirements for collective bargaining units, exclusive representative elections, and negotiation procedures covering employees at USM constituent institutions.
The bill specifically designates and structures collective bargaining units and bargaining procedures for employees and governing boards at Morgan State University.
The bill establishes specific statutory requirements governing bargaining unit composition and labor negotiations for Saint Mary's College of Maryland.
The bill specifically maintains and regulates a dedicated statutory collective bargaining unit for faculty at the Maryland School for the Deaf.
The bill explicitly maintains and regulates a separate statutory collective bargaining unit for MDTA police officers at the rank of first sergeant and below.
MES is explicitly referenced in collective bargaining statutory provisions regarding employer negotiating obligations under State Personnel and Pensions § 3-502.
The bill amends Health - General § 15-903 to update references for collective bargaining elections concerning independent home care providers under MDH programs to PERB.
The fiscal note identifies that additional Assistant Attorney General staffing is required to provide legal counsel, represent, and handle evidentiary/subpoena processes for the newly expanded PERB.
The Governor is tasked with appointing all five members and the full-time chair of the newly created Public Employee Relations Board with Senate advice and consent.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting, vetting, and processing appointments to state boards, including the newly established five-member PERB.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes qualified students aged 18 to 20 to taste alcoholic beverages in certain higher education courses without criminal penalty. Applies to students enrolled in enology, fermenting, brewing, or hospitality and tourism courses at qualified institutions of higher education. Requires students to spit out the beverage after tasting during scheduled class dates and times. Mandates that the alcoholic beverage remain under the control of an authorized instructor at least 21 years old. Exempts qualified institutions from obtaining an alcoholic beverages license if they charge no extra tasting fee. Protects participating students, instructors, and institutions from criminal penalties for furnishing, possessing, or tasting alcoholic beverages.
qa_results.responsible_party: Alcohol and Tobacco Commission; Maryland Higher Education Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Students aged 18 to 20 enrolled in enology, fermenting, brewing, or hospitality and tourism programs; authorized course instructors; and qualified Maryland institutions of higher education.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to affect State or local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill regulates educational activities and curricula (enology, fermenting, brewing, and hospitality programs) at postsecondary institutions overseen and coordinated by the Maryland Higher Education Commission.

USM institutions offering courses and degree programs in hospitality, tourism, fermenting, or brewing are directly affected, allowing students aged 18 to 20 to taste alcohol under instructor supervision without criminal penalty or additional licensing requirements.

The Comptroller regulates aspects of the alcoholic beverage industry and enforcement in Maryland; the bill creates a specific statutory exception from alcoholic beverage licensing and permitting for qualified higher education institutions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates statutory exceptions to criminal penalties under the Criminal Law Article for underage alcohol possession/consumption and adult furnishing of alcohol, which OPD defends in criminal court.
The bill carves out exceptions to misdemeanor criminal charges related to underage alcohol possession and consumption, marginally affecting judicial caseloads and court proceedings.

qa_results.bill_summary: Modifies the Family and Medical Leave Insurance Program by delaying required contributions to October 1, 2024, and benefit payments to January 1, 2026. Sets an even 50% employer and 50% employee cost-sharing split for employers with 15 or more employees. Caps the total contribution rate at 1.2% of employee wages up to the Social Security wage base. Requires the Maryland Department of Health to reimburse specified licensed or certified community service providers for employer contributions. Repeals the mandate that covered individuals exhaust employer-provided leave before receiving program benefits. Authorizes employers and covered individuals to agree to use employer-provided paid leave to replace up to 100% of average weekly wages during leave periods.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor; Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Covered employees, employers with 15 or more employees, participating self-employed individuals, and licensed or certified community service providers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures across all funds decrease by $28.7 million in FY 2024 and $10.0 million in FY 2025 due to the one-year delay in required employer contributions. General fund expenditures increase by $25.6 million in FY 2025 and by at least $35.5 million annually thereafter for Maryland Department of Health community provider reimbursements. FAMLI special fund contribution revenues and benefit expenditures are delayed by one year. Local government employer contributions are likewise deferred until October 1, 2024.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor is the primary implementing and regulatory agency responsible for administering the Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) Program, establishing contribution rates, conducting annual cost analyses, processing claims and appeals, and issuing regulations.

The bill explicitly mandates the Maryland Department of Health to reimburse certain community-based behavioral health and developmental disability service providers for their required employer contributions on at least a quarterly basis, resulting in significant fiscal impact.

The bill assigns a statutory duty to the Board of Public Works to annually monitor state employment statistics and determine whether to temporarily suspend increases in the maximum weekly benefit amount.
As the state's central personnel and budget agency, DBM is impacted by the timeline changes and funding requirements for the State's share of employer contributions for state employees.
The bill specifies that private employer plans utilizing insurance must be provided through insurers holding a certificate of authority issued by the Maryland Insurance Commissioner.
The bill statutorily references the Office of the Comptroller to report state revenue performance to the Board of Public Works when determining whether to suspend benefit increases.
The bill alters statutory provisions governing the issuance of benefit and refund checks by removing the requirement for the State Treasurer's signature.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a Class B-MGC (miniature golf course) beer, wine, and liquor license in Frederick County. Authorizes the Frederick County Board of License Commissioners to issue the license to qualifying miniature golf courses. Permits licensees to sell beer, wine, and liquor for on-premises consumption if food is offered at all times. Caps annual alcohol sales at 35% of gross sales, while requiring miniature golf and food sales of 50% and 15%. Sets an annual license fee of $1,500 and mandates an annual gross sales report for renewal.
qa_results.responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Frederick County
qa_results.stakeholders: Miniature golf courses in Frederick County and their patrons
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Frederick County revenues increase by $1,500 annually beginning in fiscal 2024 due to license fee collections. Additional county enforcement activities can be handled with existing resources. There is no state fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a local miniature golf course alcoholic beverages license administered by the Frederick County Board of License Commissioners. While the state fiscal effect is negligible, the Comptroller of Maryland is responsible for regulating the state's alcoholic beverage industry and collecting state sales and excise taxes on alcohol sales.

qa_results.bill_summary: Repeals the requirement that alcoholic beverages included in a basket of cheer in Frederick County be produced in Maryland. Applies to basket of cheer permits issued to holders of Class C per diem licenses. Retains authority to raffle up to 10 baskets of cheer as prizes at each benefit performance. Requires permit holders to obtain all alcoholic beverages for baskets from licensed retailers for off-premises consumption. Takes effect July 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Frederick County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Class C per diem alcoholic beverages license holders and benefit performance attendees in Frederick County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No State fiscal impact. Local operations and finances in Frederick County are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland oversees the regulation of the alcoholic beverage industry across the state. While this bill specifically addresses local 'basket of cheer' raffle permits administered by the Frederick County Board of License Commissioners and has no state fiscal impact, it amends the state's Alcoholic Beverages Article regarding rules on alcoholic beverage distribution and sourcing.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the quantity of alcoholic beverages an individual may consume under certain consumption permits in Frederick County. Authorizes individuals under a beer and wine consumption permit to consume three sample servings in any combination. Limits each sample to not more than two ounces of beer or one ounce of wine. Authorizes individuals under a beer, wine, and liquor consumption permit to consume three sample servings. Limits those samples to two ounces of beer, one ounce of wine, or 0.5 ounce of liquor. Maintains alternative single-serving consumption options and takes effect July 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Frederick County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Class A alcoholic beverages license holders and patrons consuming alcoholic beverages on licensed premises in Frederick County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state effect. The bill is not anticipated to materially affect Frederick County operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the state's alcohol industry. Although this legislation strictly alters allowable serving sizes under local consumption permits administered by the Frederick County Board of License Commissioners and has no state fiscal impact, it falls within the general area of state alcoholic beverage law.

qa_results.bill_summary: Repeals the restriction prohibiting the State Department of Assessments and Taxation from accepting articles of dissolution without filed personal property reports. Repeals the requirement that the Department issue a certificate of termination to a foreign corporation upon filing required reports. Allows corporations to dissolve without first filing Title 11 personal property reports. Permits foreign corporations to terminate registration or qualification without prerequisite personal property report filings. Takes effect July 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
qa_results.stakeholders: Corporations dissolving in Maryland and foreign corporations terminating Maryland registration or qualification
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: General fund revenues decrease by approximately $150,000 annually beginning in FY 2024 because an estimated 500 entities per year will no longer pay the $300 annual corporate report filing fee prior to dissolution or termination. State expenditures and local finances are not affected.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution for Police-Initiated Medium-Duty and Heavy-Duty Towing and Recovery. Requires the Department of State Police to set maximum approved towing and recovery rates by January 1, 2024. Requires tow companies on the state tow list to ban per-pound billing by October 1, 2023. Prohibits authorized tow companies from charging more than Department-approved rates for police-initiated towing and recovery. Delays the disputed-fee release requirement to March 1, 2024, until approved rates take effect. Repeals the disputed-fee release mandate upon notification that the Department has adopted approved rates.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of State Police; Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution for Police-Initiated Medium-Duty and Heavy-Duty Towing and Recovery
qa_results.stakeholders: commercial vehicle owners and operators, commercial towing businesses providing medium-duty and heavy-duty towing services, and the Department of State Police
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $44,700 in FY 2024 for one part-time administrator, increasing to $58,000 by FY 2028. Revenues are unaffected. No material local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Department of State Police with establishing approved rates for medium- and heavy-duty towing and recovery, maintaining the tow list, handling complaint resolution, and staffing the newly created Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill formally establishes a new statutory committee, the Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution for Police-Initiated Medium-Duty and Heavy-Duty Towing and Recovery.
The Administrator of the State Highway Administration is required to appoint a representative to serve on the newly created Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution.
The bill designates a seat on the Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution for a representative of the Maryland Transportation Authority Police.

The Secretary of Transportation is responsible for appointing a representative of the MDTA Police to the Committee, and the Department oversees modal administrations involved in highway clearance and safety.
The Maryland Insurance Commissioner is required to appoint a representative of the Maryland Insurance Administration to serve on the new Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the governing body of Wicomico County to create a sanitary district by ordinance or resolution. Removes Wicomico County from the list of counties exempt from State sanitary district laws. Grants created districts authority to oversee water and sewerage systems under a sanitary commission. Permits districts to issue bonds, set benefit assessments, and exercise eminent domain. Takes effect October 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Wicomico County Council
qa_results.stakeholders: Wicomico County residents, property owners with septic systems, and municipal water and sewer utilities in Wicomico County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No State fiscal effect. Wicomico County expenditures and revenues may increase if the county chooses to establish sanitary districts, but specific figures cannot currently be determined.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: House Bill 1004 amends Title 9, Subtitle 6 of the Environment Article to authorize Wicomico County to establish sanitary districts to address water, sewerage, and failing septic system issues. As the state's primary environmental regulatory agency, the Maryland Department of the Environment oversees public water and sewerage systems, county water and sewer plans, and related environmental infrastructure.

qa_results.bill_summary: Decreases the archery hunting safety zone in Howard County from 150 yards to 50 yards for qualifying archery hunters. Applies this reduction to hunters operating under a deer management permit or participating in a county-administered hunting program. Requires these hunters to shoot from an elevated position with a downward trajectory within 50 to 150 yards of specified structures. Enforces the elevation requirement near dwelling houses, residences, churches, schools, and other human-occupied buildings or camps.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources
qa_results.stakeholders: Archery hunters in Howard County hunting under a deer management permit or county-administered hunting program, as well as Howard County property owners and residents
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Natural Resources Article governing hunting safety zones and impacts hunters operating under Deer Management Permits, which are issued and regulated by the Department of Natural Resources' Wildlife and Heritage Service, and enforced by the Natural Resources Police.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits the State building code or other laws and regulations from restricting the use of certain federally approved refrigerants. Exempts regulations issued by the Maryland Department of the Environment from this prohibition. Applies when the refrigerant is designated as acceptable for use under federal law. Requires appliances containing the refrigerant to be labeled, installed, serviced, repaired, and used under federal safety standards. Defines appliances to include household or commercial air conditioners, refrigerators, chillers, and freezers.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment; Maryland Department of Labor
qa_results.stakeholders: Commercial and residential property owners, heating and cooling equipment manufacturers, HVAC and refrigeration service technicians, and local building code officials
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No material impact on State or local finances or operations. The Maryland Department of the Environment can implement the bill with existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly provides an exception for regulations issued by the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE), preserving MDE's regulatory authority over refrigerants, greenhouse gas emissions, and stratospheric ozone protection.

The Maryland Department of Labor adopts and maintains the Maryland Building Performance Standards (MBPS) and the International Mechanical Code (IMC), both of which govern building HVAC/refrigeration requirements and are directly constrained by the bill's prohibition on limiting federally approved refrigerants.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes Prince George's County to exercise eminent domain on certain neglected property. Applies to property designated as a transit-oriented development and located within a business improvement district. Excludes State-owned property from condemnation under this authority. Requires property takings to serve a public purpose, including private development consistent with a public purpose. Prohibits property takings without just compensation first paid or tendered to the entitled party. Defines transit-oriented development to include light rail stops located on the Purple Line in the county.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County
qa_results.stakeholders: Owners of abandoned, blighted, or condemned real property in Prince George's County transit-oriented development areas within business improvement districts; Prince George's County government; private developers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not directly affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly references transit-oriented developments designated under the Transportation Article as well as light rail stops along the Purple Line transit project managed within the state's transportation portfolio.
The department oversees state land use planning and smart growth initiatives, and it was consulted regarding the land use and redevelopment provisions authorized by the bill.
Eminent domain actions and contested just compensation proceedings authorized under the bill are adjudicated in Maryland's circuit courts, which are supported administratively by the agency.

qa_results.bill_summary: Grants State service credit for leave accrual rates to locally employed educational professionals who transfer to the Juvenile Services Education Program. Requires transferring professionals to be placed in comparable positions compensated at the same hourly rate of their former positions. Directs the creation of a State classification position identification number matching the individual's former salary grade. Authorizes eligible professionals transferring directly without a lapse exceeding 90 days to retain uncompensated accumulated leave balances. Applies leave accumulation and carry-over requirements of State employees upon commencement of Program employment. Applies retroactively to qualifying transfers occurring on or after July 1, 2022.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Juvenile Services; Department of Budget and Management
qa_results.stakeholders: Locally employed educational professionals from county boards of education, the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners, or county public library systems transferring to the Juvenile Services Education Program
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State operations or finances, as any operational impacts can be absorbed within existing Department of Juvenile Services resources. Local operations and finances are not directly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DJS oversees the Juvenile Services Education Program (JSEP) where these transferring educational professionals are employed, and DJS is directly responsible for operationalizing their employment, positions, and leave balances.

DBM serves as the state's central personnel agency and must assist with State classification, position numbers (PINs), and administering the special leave accrual and transfer rules established by the bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Maryland Transit Administration to submit an annual report on assaults on public transit operators. Mandates reporting to each local executive authority, county State's Attorneys, and specified General Assembly committees. Directs each report to detail assault incidents, compare multi-state data, and review transit industry best practices. Defines public transit operators to include bus, train, light rail, and subway workers, plus transit station managers. Requires the initial December 1, 2023 report to evaluate local safety policies and five-year assault data.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Transit Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Public transit operators and transit station managers employed by the Maryland Transit Administration, the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority, or local political subdivisions; county and municipal local executive authorities; county State's Attorneys
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Transportation Trust Fund expenditures increase by $50,000 in FY 2024 only for expert consultant costs to evaluate the feasibility of establishing a statewide local transit safety officer. Other reporting requirements are absorbed within existing resources. No effect on State revenues. Local governments can provide data and receive reports within existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 1049 directly mandates that the Maryland Transit Administration (MTA) compile and submit an annual report detailing assaults on public transit operators, conduct multi-state comparative analyses, evaluate safety technologies, and examine the feasibility of establishing a statewide local transit safety officer, with an estimated $50,000 fiscal impact in FY 2024.

As the parent department of the Maryland Transit Administration, the Maryland Department of Transportation oversees the modal administration's operations and finances the bill's implementation costs through the Transportation Trust Fund.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes an applicant to appeal a decision issued by the State Public Information Act Compliance Board to the circuit court. Provides that an appeal automatically stays the Board's decision pending the circuit court's determination. Specifies venue in the county where the applicant resides or has a principal place of business for certain board decisions. Authorizes a party aggrieved by the circuit court's final judgment to appeal to the Appellate Court of Maryland.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Public Information Act Compliance Board; Maryland Judiciary
qa_results.stakeholders: Public Information Act applicants, complainants, public record custodians, and state and local governmental units
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly governs the decisions and appeals process of the State Public Information Act Compliance Board (PIACB), which is a state board established to review and resolve disputes under the Public Information Act.

The bill alters judicial review procedures by clarifying filing venues and authorizing applicants to appeal PIACB decisions to the circuit courts and further appeal final judgments to the Appellate Court of Maryland.

The Office of the Attorney General provides staff support and legal counsel to the Public Information Act Compliance Board, publishes the State's PIA Manual, and represents state agencies in litigation concerning public record disputes.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a performing arts theater beer and wine license in Harford County. Authorizes the Harford County Board of License Commissioners to issue the license to nonprofit-operated theaters. Allows license holders to sell beer and wine for on-premises consumption during performances, intermissions, and designated receptions. Requires license holders to offer snacks for sale whenever beer and wine are sold. Mandates that license holders purchase beer and wine from authorized licensed wholesalers. Sets the annual license fee at $500 effective July 1, 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Harford County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: nonprofit organizations operating performing arts theaters in Harford County, theater patrons, and licensed beer and wine wholesalers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Harford County revenues increase by $500 annually beginning in fiscal 2024 from the issuance of one license. Additional county enforcement can be handled with existing resources. There is no state fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland oversees state regulation of the alcohol industry, including licensed alcohol wholesalers from whom licensees under this bill are required to purchase beer and wine, although direct licensing and local fee collection are handled by Harford County.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the population quota used to determine the maximum number of certain off-sale alcoholic beverages licenses in Harford County. Increases the population threshold from 3,000 individuals to 4,000 individuals per license. Prohibits issuing more than one Class A, Class A-1, or Class A-2 license per 4,000 county residents. Bars new license issuance when a class exceeds the quota until revocation or surrender creates a vacancy. Excludes the transfer, conversion, or renewal of an existing license from these quota restrictions.
qa_results.responsible_party: Harford County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Class A, Class A-1, and Class A-2 alcoholic beverages license applicants and license holders in Harford County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No state fiscal effect. Harford County finances and operations are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill references population metrics as specified by the Maryland Department of Health to determine the quota formula used for issuing certain alcoholic beverages licenses in Harford County.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes 6-day and 7-day Class HC beer and wine licenses in Harford County. Authorizes the Board of License Commissioners for Harford County to issue licenses to qualifying health club facilities. Requires qualifying clubs to have at least 150 dues-paying members and swimming pools or pickleball courts. Authorizes license holders to sell beer and wine for on-premises consumption from 1 p.m. to 9 p.m. Requires license holders to provide prepackaged food or snacks whenever beer and wine are sold. Exempts Class HC licenses from distance restrictions regarding places of worship and schools.
qa_results.responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Harford County
qa_results.stakeholders: health clubs and health club members in Harford County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Harford County revenues increase by an estimated $1,400 annually beginning in fiscal 2024 based on the issuance of one 7-day license. Local enforcement costs can be absorbed with existing resources, and State finances are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller regulates the state's alcoholic beverage industry. Although this legislation specifically pertains to local licensing administered by the Harford County Board of License Commissioners with no state fiscal impact, it relates to the broader regulation and distribution of alcoholic beverages from licensed wholesalers.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Commission on Hate Crime Response and Prevention in the Office of the Attorney General. Requires the Attorney General to appoint commission members representing designated advocacy organizations, law enforcement, and the public. Directs the commission to develop prevention and response strategies and evaluate State hate crime laws and policies. Requires annual reports by December 1, beginning in 2024, to the State Department of Education and the General Assembly. Mandates annual State budget funding beginning in fiscal year 2025 for a full-time assistant Attorney General.
qa_results.responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General; Commission on Hate Crime Response and Prevention
qa_results.stakeholders: victims of hate crimes, community advocacy and civil rights organizations, law enforcement agencies, and Maryland public school students and educators
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Federal fund expenditures increase by $114,400 in FY 2024 for a contractual assistant Attorney General. General fund expenditures increase by $136,300 in FY 2025 for a permanent assistant Attorney General and ongoing operating costs under a mandated appropriation. State revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 1066 establishes the Commission on Hate Crime Response and Prevention within the Office of the Attorney General (OAG). The Attorney General appoints members, serves as chair (or designates a chair), and OAG provides staff for the commission, with direct fiscal impacts for personnel and operational costs.
